  "title": "Workload-forecast-based headroom controller for Dedicated capacity",
  "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Workload-forecast-based headroom controller for Dedicated capacity\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/business-ops/ENG-62670-workload-forecast-headroom-controller.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: business-ops\nProject: Dedicated-Autoscale-Next\nTeam: engineering\n\ncause reactive overprovisioning or missed SLOs before scaling completes, and (2) cost-inefficient oscillations when traffic rapidly changes. Several related tickets implemented safety envelopes and conservative stepping, but none incorporate predictive headroom. Customer complaints from three enterprise Dedicated tenants noted latency regressions during predictable marketing spikes.\n\nProposed Solution: Build a lightweight forecasting module (exponential smoothing + seasonality detector) in the autoscaler service to predict 1-30min horizon throughput and tail latency proxies. Compute a headroom target: predicted_peak * safety_margin + min_capacity. Use an adaptive controller that translates headroom delta into scale actions with a PI-inspired controller, but capped by per-tenant hard limits and global fleet safety windows. Integrate a circuit-breaker that prevents scaling above emergency ceiling unless sustained over 2 minutes. Provide knobs: forecast_horizon, safety_margin_pct, max_step_percent, cooldown_s, and emergency_ceiling. Expose metrics and a dashboard and add canary rollout to 5% of Dedicated clusters.\n\n## Decisions\n\n- Use single-model ETS (error-trend-seasonality) style forecasting implemented in Go for low latency and deterministic resource use\n  - Forecast horizons: default 5 minutes; configurable up to 30 minutes per project\n  - Controller algorithm: PI-inspired mapping of headroom delta to steps with exponential backoff on repeated failures\n  - Safety limits: per-tenant floor/ceiling plus a cross-tenant emergency ceiling enforced by fleet controller\n  - Circuit-breaker triggers require predicted headroom > emergency_ceiling OR observed sustained p95 breach for >120s\n  - No immediate autoscale-down on short negative forecast spikes: require sustained 3x check intervals before reduction\n\n## Tradeoffs",

  "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Composite-target scaling governor: safe multi-metric autoscaling policy and runtime controls\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-100019-composite-target-governor-policy-spec.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: engineering\nProject: Dedicated Capacity Autoscaling\nTeam: engineering\n\n(b) p95/p99 latency headroom for tail-sensitive workloads, (c) GPU occupancy and kv-cache hit rate for memory-sensitive models, and (d) queue depth and RPS for short requests. Each metric normalized to 0..1 and expressed with a confidence window (decay/exponential smoothing).\n\n2) Multi-algorithm scaling pipeline: implement a two-stage controller: a predictive warmup stage (lightweight time-series forecasting + short-horizon ML model) to request proactive capacity during predictable demand ramps; and a conservative closed-loop stage (PID-derived proportional+derivative with quantile targeting) to make incremental adjustments against the composite score. The closed-loop stage enforces min-step and max-step limits.\n\n3) Safety limits and fences: slope limit (max % change per 5m), surge budget ledger (per-tenant and fleet-level credits), minimum committed baseline (never scale below reserved throughput), and emergency kill-switch that falls back to lower-cost model variants or throttles non-critical tenants. Include rollback triggers when error rates or eviction counts exceed thresholds.\n\n4) Policy DSL and templating: a compact policy spec that lets operators pick target composition, algorithm parameters (PID gains, forecast horizon), and safety envelopes. Provide policy presets: \"conservative-stability\", \"balanced-latency\", \"aggressive-burst\". Policies discoverable in Console with preview simulations.\n\n5) Observability and verification: new telemetry streams (composite_score, predicted_headroom, step_recommendation, applied_delta) emitted with each decision. Dashboards: per-fleet and per-tenant views, histograms for step sizes, and heatmaps for policy activation. Add an offline simulator to replay traces (synthetic + past production) and compute safety metrics (SLA breach probability, cost delta, oscillation index).\n\n6) Rollout plan: start with read-only decision recommendations for a set of staging fleets, then opt-in closed-loop for low-risk tenants, followed by gradual expansion with automatic rollback on safety violations.",

3) Caching + consistency

(This is a tradeoff; see Risks.)

  "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Concurrency Governor: Hybrid Scaling Algorithm & Safety Limits for Dedicated Fleets\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-77421-concurrency-governor-scaling-limiter.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: engineering\nProject: Dedicated Capacity - Autoscaling\nTeam: engineering\n\nobserved concurrency and latency, and a saturating rate limiter that caps scale-up and scale-down velocity. The governor exposes tunable knobs: concurrency_target, headroom_multiplier, max_surge_ratio, min_capacity_floor, and cooldown_window. Runtime will emit debug traces for decisions and contribute to the Console rollouts dashboard.\n\nAlgorithm Details: - Inputs: arrival_rate (requests/sec), observed_concurrency, avg_token_time, KV_cache_hit_ratio, per-tenant reserved_capacity.\n- Predictive estimator: 30s EWMA on arrival_rate and short linear extrapolation to estimate 60s demand.\n- Reactive controller: error = target_concurrency - observed_concurrency; output delta_capacity = Kp*error + Ki*integral(error) (bounded).\n- Velocity limiter: enforce max_scale_up = floor(current_capacity * max_surge_ratio) and max_scale_down = floor(current_capacity * (1 - min_capacity_floor)).\n- Fallbacks: if GPU queue depth > threshold for >30s, route to burst pool if allowed; else trigger paired throttling policy.\n- Configuration: default concurrency_target derived from tenant SLA and model sequence length distribution.\n\nSafety Limits: - Hard caps: max_surge_ratio default 1.25 (25% instantaneous surge), absolute max 2.0 only for flagged enterprise tenants.\n- Min capacity floor: 60% of reserved commit to prevent deep undershoots.\n- Cooldown window: 45s minimum between successive scale adjustments for same pool.\n- Oscillation detector: if >3 direction changes in 5 minutes, halve control gains and emit incident for SRE review.\n- Cost guard: track estimated token spend per minute; if projected 10-minute spend exceeds budget threshold, governor reduces non-critical tenants by proportion until under budget.",

Title: Workload-forecast-based headroom controller for Dedicated capacity
Source: EnterpriseRAG/linear
Path: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/business-ops/ENG-62670-workload-forecast-headroom-controller.json
Connector: linear
Workspace: business-ops
Project: Dedicated-Autoscale-Next
Team: engineering

cause reactive overprovisioning or missed SLOs before scaling completes, and (2) cost-inefficient oscillations when traffic rapidly changes. Several related tickets implemented safety envelopes and conservative stepping, but none incorporate predictive headroom. Customer complaints from three enterprise Dedicated tenants noted latency regressions during predictable marketing spikes.

Proposed Solution: Build a lightweight forecasting module (exponential smoothing + seasonality detector) in the autoscaler service to predict 1-30min horizon throughput and tail latency proxies. Compute a headroom target: predicted_peak * safety_margin + min_capacity. Use an adaptive controller that translates headroom delta into scale actions with a PI-inspired controller, but capped by per-tenant hard limits and global fleet safety windows. Integrate a circuit-breaker that prevents scaling above emergency ceiling unless sustained over 2 minutes. Provide knobs: forecast_horizon, safety_margin_pct, max_step_percent, cooldown_s, and emergency_ceiling. Expose metrics and a dashboard and add canary rollout to 5% of Dedicated clusters.

## Decisions

- Use single-model ETS (error-trend-seasonality) style forecasting implemented in Go for low latency and deterministic resource use
  - Forecast horizons: default 5 minutes; configurable up to 30 minutes per project
  - Controller algorithm: PI-inspired mapping of headroom delta to steps with exponential backoff on repeated failures
  - Safety limits: per-tenant floor/ceiling plus a cross-tenant emergency ceiling enforced by fleet controller
  - Circuit-breaker triggers require predicted headroom > emergency_ceiling OR observed sustained p95 breach for >120s
  - No immediate autoscale-down on short negative forecast spikes: require sustained 3x check intervals before reduction

## Tradeoffs

(b) p95/p99 latency headroom for tail-sensitive workloads, (c) GPU occupancy and kv-cache hit rate for memory-sensitive models, and (d) queue depth and RPS for short requests. Each metric normalized to 0..1 and expressed with a confidence window (decay/exponential smoothing).

2) Multi-algorithm scaling pipeline: implement a two-stage controller: a predictive warmup stage (lightweight time-series forecasting + short-horizon ML model) to request proactive capacity during predictable demand ramps; and a conservative closed-loop stage (PID-derived proportional+derivative with quantile targeting) to make incremental adjustments against the composite score. The closed-loop stage enforces min-step and max-step limits.

3) Safety limits and fences: slope limit (max % change per 5m), surge budget ledger (per-tenant and fleet-level credits), minimum committed baseline (never scale below reserved throughput), and emergency kill-switch that falls back to lower-cost model variants or throttles non-critical tenants. Include rollback triggers when error rates or eviction counts exceed thresholds.

4) Policy DSL and templating: a compact policy spec that lets operators pick target composition, algorithm parameters (PID gains, forecast horizon), and safety envelopes. Provide policy presets: "conservative-stability", "balanced-latency", "aggressive-burst". Policies discoverable in Console with preview simulations.

5) Observability and verification: new telemetry streams (composite_score, predicted_headroom, step_recommendation, applied_delta) emitted with each decision. Dashboards: per-fleet and per-tenant views, histograms for step sizes, and heatmaps for policy activation. Add an offline simulator to replay traces (synthetic + past production) and compute safety metrics (SLA breach probability, cost delta, oscillation index).

6) Rollout plan: start with read-only decision recommendations for a set of staging fleets, then opt-in closed-loop for low-risk tenants, followed by gradual expansion with automatic rollback on safety violations.

- For bounds:

Implementation plan
1) Flag source
- Use Control Plane feature gate service (FeatureGate) as the single source of truth.
- Provide evaluation by account_id and optional deployment_id.
- Autoscaler will fetch a signed/effective gate snapshot for each deployment on a TTL (60s) to avoid hot-path network dependency.

2) Data model / API
- Add "effective_gates" to the autoscaler decision context (not persisted long-term).
- Include a "gate_snapshot_id" (hash) in scaling decision audit events so we can correlate incidents to the flag state.

3) Caching + consistency
- Autoscaler caches flags with:
  - TTL: 60s
  - jitter: +/- 10s to avoid herd refresh
  - hard max age: 5m (after which fail closed to defaults; see Failure modes)
- Control plane caches can be longer (5m) but must reflect global kill switch within 60s.

4) Failure modes / safe defaults
- If the feature gate service is unavailable:
  - Treat gates as disabled (fail closed) for both bounds and predictive mode.
  - Exception: if bounds were already actively enforced for a deployment and the gate snapshot cannot be refreshed, continue using the last known gate state for up to 5m to avoid flapping; after 5m, log error and fail closed to disabled (reverting to current behavior). (This is a tradeoff; see Risks.)
- If the kill switch value cannot be fetched, assume kill switch is ON (predictive disabled) but keep bounds gating based on last known state (since bounds are a safety guardrail rather than a risk factor).

result.title: Concurrency Governor: Hybrid Scaling Algorithm & Safety Limits for Dedicated Fleets
result.text:
[Document context]
Title: Concurrency Governor: Hybrid Scaling Algorithm & Safety Limits for Dedicated Fleets
Source: EnterpriseRAG/linear
Path: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-77421-concurrency-governor-scaling-limiter.json
Connector: linear
Workspace: engineering
Project: Dedicated Capacity - Autoscaling
Team: engineering

observed concurrency and latency, and a saturating rate limiter that caps scale-up and scale-down velocity. The governor exposes tunable knobs: concurrency_target, headroom_multiplier, max_surge_ratio, min_capacity_floor, and cooldown_window. Runtime will emit debug traces for decisions and contribute to the Console rollouts dashboard.

Algorithm Details: - Inputs: arrival_rate (requests/sec), observed_concurrency, avg_token_time, KV_cache_hit_ratio, per-tenant reserved_capacity.
- Predictive estimator: 30s EWMA on arrival_rate and short linear extrapolation to estimate 60s demand.
- Reactive controller: error = target_concurrency - observed_concurrency; output delta_capacity = Kp*error + Ki*integral(error) (bounded).
- Velocity limiter: enforce max_scale_up = floor(current_capacity * max_surge_ratio) and max_scale_down = floor(current_capacity * (1 - min_capacity_floor)).
- Fallbacks: if GPU queue depth > threshold for >30s, route to burst pool if allowed; else trigger paired throttling policy.
- Configuration: default concurrency_target derived from tenant SLA and model sequence length distribution.

Safety Limits: - Hard caps: max_surge_ratio default 1.25 (25% instantaneous surge), absolute max 2.0 only for flagged enterprise tenants.
- Min capacity floor: 60% of reserved commit to prevent deep undershoots.
- Cooldown window: 45s minimum between successive scale adjustments for same pool.
- Oscillation detector: if >3 direction changes in 5 minutes, halve control gains and emit incident for SRE review.
- Cost guard: track estimated token spend per minute; if projected 10-minute spend exceeds budget threshold, governor reduces non-critical tenants by proportion until under budget.

This is configurable via autoscaler policy fields: anticipatory.enabled (bool), anticipatory.window_seconds (int), anticipatory.grace_seconds (int), anticipatory.saturation_threshold (float). 2) Throttle fence: reconciler-level fencing around burst-credit reconciliation ensures only one in-flight reconciliation per tenant/fleet pair; this prevents two concurrent controllers (e.g. during leader handover or canary) from both deducting the same soft burst credits and oversubscribing. Fence semantics are optimistic-lease-based with a short TTL to avoid permanent locks during failover. 3) Saturation-aware backfill: when a short-term deficit is detected, the reconciler will prefer backfill from the warm-pool and deferred soft credits before hard provisioning, and will emit a new telemetry dimension (reconciled_burst_source) describing whether capacity came from warm-pool, deferred_credit, or new_provision. Rollout strategy: feature gated behind OPT_IN policy flag; default off for existing clusters. We perform a staged rollout: first enable on the perf-canary cluster with a single canary tenant, then ramp to 10% of traffic with metrics baseline checks, then full rollout if no regression. - Metrics: admission_decisions{allow,degrade,reject} by tenant_region_tier

Customer complaints from three enterprise Dedicated tenants noted latency regressions during predictable marketing spikes.\n\nProposed Solution: Build a lightweight forecasting module (exponential smoothing + seasonality detector) in the autoscaler service to predict 1-30min horizon throughput and tail latency proxies. (2) An autoscaler termination-healthcheck regression (introduced in autoscaler v1.14) caused GPU pods to be killed and recreated under load rather than gracefully draining, creating cache churn and transient OOMs which increased latency and reduced capacity.

Contributing Factors: - Canary tests lacked a specific slice of real-world prompt patterns (long-chained context prompts) where the tokenizer change mattered.
- Autoscaler health-check change removed a small sleep/drain that previously allowed KV cache eviction to complete; this increased cache misses and GPU memory pressure.
- Release process allowed v3.1 to be promoted from canary to gradual rollout before full slice coverage.
- Monitoring thresholds for pod restart rate were low-sensitivity and didn't automatically pause rollouts.
- No automated e2e rerank quality gate for top-K recall in the deployment pipeline.

Immediate Mitigation: - Rolled back reranker to v3.0 within 35 minutes of detection.
- Reconfigured autoscaler to use the previous termination behavior and increased drain timeout, preventing further pod flapping.
- Shifted high-priority customer traffic to warm pool instances with pre-warmed KV caches.
- Enabled temporary rate limiting for non-critical backgrounds rerank jobs to reduce pressure on GPU pools.

Long Term Remediation: - Add a dedicated 'long-context' test slice to canary evaluation covering tokenizer edge-cases and long-chain prompts.
- Implement a top-K recall quality gate (automated) that blocks rollouts if regression > 3% on production-like prompt sets.
- Revert and fix autoscaler termination logic; add a unit and integration test ensuring graceful KV cache drain on termination.
- Introduce an autoscaler rollback circuit breaker: if restart rate > X within Y minutes, pause rollouts and notify owners.
- Create a warm-pool autoscaling policy to keep a small number of GPU pods always pre-warmed with KV caches for low-latency failover.
- Update runbooks and SLO alerts to include combined latency+quality heuristics to surface model regressions faster.

Title: Autoscaler sensitivity regression: HPA/KEDA misfires causing capacity oscillation
Source: EnterpriseRAG/linear

10-30s) to KEDA, which triggered scale-up events. HPA was configured to aggressively scale down based on CPU with a short stabilization window, producing a feedback loop: KEDA scale-ups followed by rapid HPA scale-downs, causing pod churn and increased cold-start latency.

## Contributing Factors

- Metric exporter change removed smoothing that filtered transient bursts
  - KEDA was using un-smoothed queue depth with a short polling interval (5s)
  - HPA downscale stabilization was too aggressive (30s) and used CPU which lags compared to queue metrics
  - No canary rollout of metrics change; change deployed to all regions simultaneously
  - Warm pool size for realtime-inference was minimal; pod startup cold-start penalty is ~600ms per replica
  - Runbook lacked a specific section mapping KEDA/HPA interactions for queue-based autoscaling

## Mitigations Taken

- Rolled back metric exporter PR #1876 to restore 60s smoothing
  - Increased minReplicas from 2 to 4 during incident window to maintain warm capacity
  - Adjusted KEDA polling interval from 5s to 15s as a temporary band-aid
  - Updated alert thresholds to surface pod churn (scale events per minute) earlier

## Permanent Fixes And Decisions

- Restore smoothing by default in the metric exporter and make the smoothing window configurable; default=60s
  - Introduce percentile-based HPA metric for CPU (p95) instead of average to better reflect tail pressure
  - Adjust HPA downscale stabilization to 3 minutes and add cooldown to avoid immediate downscales after KEDA scale-ups
  - Add a small warm pool (reserved replicas) for realtime-inference with gradual autoscale bypass for the pool
  - Change KEDA polling interval default for queue-backed scalers to 15s and add jitter to avoid synchronized triggers
  - Require canary rollout (10% traffic for 30m with automatic rollback) for metric/telemetry changes

## Action Items",

9) Predictor stale (timestamp too old)

- Expected behavior:
  - If forecast age > staleness threshold:
    - ignore predictive input, fall back to reactive.
    - optionally emit event “predictive_disabled_due_to_staleness”.
  - Do NOT keep using stale forecast for scale-down decisions.
- Alert:
  - prediction_staleness_seconds > threshold for pilots.

10) Predictor overestimates (false positives) → overscale
- Symptom:
  - Capacity jumps up but demand doesn’t arrive. Cost spike; possibly impacts fleet availability.
- Expected behavior:
  - Anti-oscillation: conservative step sizes for predictive-only scale-ups; require confidence threshold.
  - Use cooldowns; allow scale-down slowly and only to min.
  - If prediction error high for a rolling window, auto-disable predictive for that deployment (fail open to reactive) for a fixed backoff period.
- Observability:
  - prediction_error (MAPE / absolute error) per deployment (careful with cardinality).
  - Metric: predictive_auto_disabled_total{reason=error_high}.",

Title: anticipatory-resize-policy-and-tenant-throttle-fence

Connector: github
Workspace: redwood

Description: Context: customer fleets have become sensitive to repeated rapid scale-in events that withdraw headroom too aggressively, causing short-lived saturation and increased tail latency. Motivation: reduce oscillation during transient drops while preserving the ability to grant short-term burst capacity when warranted. This PR adds an "anticipatory resize" policy that delays scale-in decisions based on a saturation-aware prediction window, and a tenant-level "throttle fence" that serializes competing credit reconciliations to avoid double-counting burst capacity. Design summary: 1) Anticipatory resize: a lightweight moving-window predictor samples per-tenant utilization percentiles (P50/P95), current queue depth, and warm-pool fill ratio to compute a short horizon demand estimate. Rather than immediately reducing shard counts when utilization dips, the controller enters a guarded cooldown that only commits scale-in if the prediction window remains below the target for a configured grace period. This is configurable via autoscaler policy fields: anticipatory.enabled (bool), anticipatory.window_seconds (int), anticipatory.grace_seconds (int), anticipatory.saturation_threshold (float). 2) Throttle fence: reconciler-level fencing around burst-credit reconciliation ensures only one in-flight reconciliation per tenant/fleet pair; this prevents two concurrent controllers (e.g. during leader handover or canary) from both deducting the same soft burst credits and oversubscribing. Fence semantics are optimistic-lease-based with a short TTL to avoid permanent locks during failover. 3) Saturation-aware backfill: when a short-term deficit is detected, the reconciler will prefer backfill from the warm-pool and deferred soft credits before hard provisioning, and will emit a new telemetry dimension (reconciled_burst_source) describing whether capacity came from warm-pool, deferred_credit, or new_provision. Rollout strategy: feature gated behind OPT_IN policy flag; default off for existing clusters. We perform a staged rollout: first enable on the perf-canary cluster with a single canary tenant, then ramp to 10% of traffic with metrics baseline checks, then full rollout if no regression. Backwards compatibility: controllers that don't support anticipatory fields will ignore them. Implementation notes: -

## Tradeoffs And Risks

- Increased decision latency if admission service is synchronous — mitigate with local fast-path caches of token-bucket state

## Monitoring And Alerting

  - Shed_rate: fraction of requests that hit each degradation mode
  - Quality_signals: fallback_model_rate and eval-quality-regressions for canonical prompts

  - Expand to additional regions with progressively increasing traffic share, run chaos for each expansion

Title: Workload-forecast-based headroom controller for Dedicated capacity
Source: EnterpriseRAG/linear

Connector: linear
Workspace: business-ops
Project: Dedicated-Autoscale-Next
Team: engineering

cause reactive overprovisioning or missed SLOs before scaling completes, and (2) cost-inefficient oscillations when traffic rapidly changes. Several related tickets implemented safety envelopes and conservative stepping, but none incorporate predictive headroom. Customer complaints from three enterprise Dedicated tenants noted latency regressions during predictable marketing spikes.

Proposed Solution: Build a lightweight forecasting module (exponential smoothing + seasonality detector) in the autoscaler service to predict 1-30min horizon throughput and tail latency proxies. Compute a headroom target: predicted_peak * safety_margin + min_capacity. Use an adaptive controller that translates headroom delta into scale actions with a PI-inspired controller, but capped by per-tenant hard limits and global fleet safety windows. Integrate a circuit-breaker that prevents scaling above emergency ceiling unless sustained over 2 minutes. Provide knobs: forecast_horizon, safety_margin_pct, max_step_percent, cooldown_s, and emergency_ceiling. Expose metrics and a dashboard and add canary rollout to 5% of Dedicated clusters.

## Decisions

- Use single-model ETS (error-trend-seasonality) style forecasting implemented in Go for low latency and deterministic resource use
  - Forecast horizons: default 5 minutes; configurable up to 30 minutes per project
  - Controller algorithm: PI-inspired mapping of headroom delta to steps with exponential backoff on repeated failures
  - Safety limits: per-tenant floor/ceiling plus a cross-tenant emergency ceiling enforced by fleet controller
  - Circuit-breaker triggers require predicted headroom > emergency_ceiling OR observed sustained p95 breach for >120s
  - No immediate autoscale-down on short negative forecast spikes: require sustained 3x check intervals before reduction

## Tradeoffs

(2) An autoscaler termination-healthcheck regression (introduced in autoscaler v1.14) caused GPU pods to be killed and recreated under load rather than gracefully draining, creating cache churn and transient OOMs which increased latency and reduced capacity.

Contributing Factors: - Canary tests lacked a specific slice of real-world prompt patterns (long-chained context prompts) where the tokenizer change mattered.
- Autoscaler health-check change removed a small sleep/drain that previously allowed KV cache eviction to complete; this increased cache misses and GPU memory pressure.
- Release process allowed v3.1 to be promoted from canary to gradual rollout before full slice coverage.
- Monitoring thresholds for pod restart rate were low-sensitivity and didn't automatically pause rollouts.
- No automated e2e rerank quality gate for top-K recall in the deployment pipeline.

Immediate Mitigation: - Rolled back reranker to v3.0 within 35 minutes of detection.
- Reconfigured autoscaler to use the previous termination behavior and increased drain timeout, preventing further pod flapping.
- Shifted high-priority customer traffic to warm pool instances with pre-warmed KV caches.
- Enabled temporary rate limiting for non-critical backgrounds rerank jobs to reduce pressure on GPU pools.

Long Term Remediation: - Add a dedicated 'long-context' test slice to canary evaluation covering tokenizer edge-cases and long-chain prompts.
- Implement a top-K recall quality gate (automated) that blocks rollouts if regression > 3% on production-like prompt sets.
- Revert and fix autoscaler termination logic; add a unit and integration test ensuring graceful KV cache drain on termination.
- Introduce an autoscaler rollback circuit breaker: if restart rate > X within Y minutes, pause rollouts and notify owners.
- Create a warm-pool autoscaling policy to keep a small number of GPU pods always pre-warmed with KV caches for low-latency failover.
- Update runbooks and SLO alerts to include combined latency+quality heuristics to surface model regressions faster.

Description: Context: We currently rely on simple token-rate ceilings and percentile-based utilization for tenant throttling and autoscaler decisions. This leads to two operational gaps: 1) sudden bursty tenants can repeatedly cause short-lived tail latencies and capacity churn, and 2) our utilization signals (avg/p90) do not capture temporal volatility which is useful for preemptive autoscaling. Motivation: Introduce a lightweight runtime 'rate envelope' controller that enforces soft per-tenant concurrency/throughput envelopes with graceful degradation and backoff, and add a 'utilization entropy' reporter that quantifies temporal variability in per-tenant utilization to inform the autoscaler and the operations dashboard. High level changes: - New runtime controller pkg/autoscaler/rate_envelope_controller.go that enforces tenant envelopes and exposes a ranked violation metric. Envelope semantics are soft: requests that would exceed the envelope are accepted where possible but marked for best-effort throttling and may be routed to a lower-cost variant when SLA tier allows. - Utilization entropy reporter at pkg/telemetry/util_entropy_reporter.go that computes a rolling entropy-like score over time-bucketed utilization histograms (per-tenant, per-pool) and emits metrics util.entropy{tenant, pool} and util.entropy_percentile. - Autoscaler integration: the dedicated autoscaler now ingests util.entropy and uses a hysteresis-weighted scaling factor to favour scale-up on high-entropy tenants. Implementation notes and knobs: - rate_envelope is configurable via tenant config: envelope.max_concurrency, envelope.max_tokens_per_sec, envelope.penalty_backoff_ms. Defaults mimic current soft-burst limits but add a decay window. - util_entropy uses 1m buckets by default, 12-bucket rolling window (12 minutes), config at telem.entropy.window_size and telem.entropy.buckets. - A new admin API endpoint /admin/tenants/{id}/envelope lets SRE inspect and override envelopes for an incident. Rollout plan: 1) Feature gated, default off for existing Dedicated customers. 2) Enable for a small pilot pool (canary) for 48h with increased telemetry retention. 3) Gradual ramp across remaining dedicated

result.text:
[Document context]
Title: Autoscaler sensitivity regression: HPA/KEDA misfires causing capacity oscillation
Source: EnterpriseRAG/linear
Path: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-93421-autoscaler-sensitivity-regression-root-cause-action-plan.json
Connector: linear
Workspace: engineering
Project: autoscaling-reliability
Team: engineering

10-30s) to KEDA, which triggered scale-up events. HPA was configured to aggressively scale down based on CPU with a short stabilization window, producing a feedback loop: KEDA scale-ups followed by rapid HPA scale-downs, causing pod churn and increased cold-start latency.

## Contributing Factors

- Metric exporter change removed smoothing that filtered transient bursts
  - KEDA was using un-smoothed queue depth with a short polling interval (5s)
  - HPA downscale stabilization was too aggressive (30s) and used CPU which lags compared to queue metrics
  - No canary rollout of metrics change; change deployed to all regions simultaneously
  - Warm pool size for realtime-inference was minimal; pod startup cold-start penalty is ~600ms per replica
  - Runbook lacked a specific section mapping KEDA/HPA interactions for queue-based autoscaling

## Mitigations Taken

- Rolled back metric exporter PR #1876 to restore 60s smoothing
  - Increased minReplicas from 2 to 4 during incident window to maintain warm capacity
  - Adjusted KEDA polling interval from 5s to 15s as a temporary band-aid
  - Updated alert thresholds to surface pod churn (scale events per minute) earlier

## Permanent Fixes And Decisions

- Restore smoothing by default in the metric exporter and make the smoothing window configurable; default=60s
  - Introduce percentile-based HPA metric for CPU (p95) instead of average to better reflect tail pressure
  - Adjust HPA downscale stabilization to 3 minutes and add cooldown to avoid immediate downscales after KEDA scale-ups
  - Add a small warm pool (reserved replicas) for realtime-inference with gradual autoscale bypass for the pool
  - Change KEDA polling interval default for queue-backed scalers to 15s and add jitter to avoid synchronized triggers
  - Require canary rollout (10% traffic for 30m with automatic rollback) for metric/telemetry changes

8) Predictor returns null / NaN / negative / out-of-range
- Symptom:
  - Forecast service bug or missing data.
- Expected behavior:
  - Treat as “prediction unavailable”; do not use value.
  - Fall back to reactive scaling only.
  - Never let null translate to 0 desired (explicit guard).
- Observability:
  - Metric: prediction_invalid_total{reason=null|nan|negative|too_large}.
  - Include predictor_version + model_id in logs for correlation.

9) Predictor stale (timestamp too old)
- Symptom:
  - Forecast pipeline lag; values are old.
- Expected behavior:
  - If forecast age > staleness threshold:
    - ignore predictive input, fall back to reactive.
    - optionally emit event “predictive_disabled_due_to_staleness”.
  - Do NOT keep using stale forecast for scale-down decisions.
- Alert:
  - prediction_staleness_seconds > threshold for pilots.

10) Predictor overestimates (false positives) → overscale
- Symptom:
  - Capacity jumps up but demand doesn’t arrive. Cost spike; possibly impacts fleet availability.
- Expected behavior:
  - Anti-oscillation: conservative step sizes for predictive-only scale-ups; require confidence threshold.
  - Use cooldowns; allow scale-down slowly and only to min.
  - If prediction error high for a rolling window, auto-disable predictive for that deployment (fail open to reactive) for a fixed backoff period.
- Observability:
  - prediction_error (MAPE / absolute error) per deployment (careful with cardinality).
  - Metric: predictive_auto_disabled_total{reason=error_high}.

  - prediction_error (MAPE / absolute error) per deployment (careful with cardinality).

## Failure injection scenarios
Each scenario includes: setup, injection, expected behavior, rollback/cleanup.

### Scenario A: Forecast outage (predictor unreachable)
Setup:
- Predictive mode enabled for test deployment.
Injection:
- Block forecast provider calls (simulate network policy drop) OR return 5xx from provider for 10 minutes.
Expected:
- Autoscaler falls back to reactive scaling within 1–2 evaluation intervals.
- No unsafe scale-down; min bound continues to be honored.
- A clear metric/log indicates fallback state and reason ("prediction_unavailable").
- Alert: Warning-level (not page) if outage < 15m; page only if sustained and associated with queue buildup (per SLO doc).
Rollback:
- Remove block / restore provider; confirm predictive resumes after freshness check passes.

### Scenario B: Stale forecast (forecast present but too old)
Setup:
- Predictive mode enabled; provider returns last-known forecast.
Injection:
- Freeze forecast updates; allow age to exceed staleness threshold.
Expected:
- Autoscaler ignores stale forecast and uses reactive.
- Observability shows forecast age and fallback reason ("prediction_stale").
- No oscillation when transitioning modes.
Rollback:
- Restore updates; verify resume.

### Scenario C: Bad forecast (systematic under-prediction during ramp)
Setup:
- Configure a known ramp (e.g., +30% QPS every 5 minutes for 30 minutes).
Injection:
- Provide forecast that is ~50% lower than actual.
Expected:
- Reactive saturation/queue depth overrides prediction (while respecting max bound).
- If max bound is hit, we should see:
  - bounded desired == max
  - sustained queue depth signal
  - max-bound saturation alert triggers at configured threshold
  - runbook path is clear (raise max, add capacity, or enable graceful degradation via routing)
Rollback:
- Restore accurate forecast; ramp down traffic.",

---

### P1 Paging: Sustained queue buildup while max-bound hit
**Condition:** max_bound_hit = true AND (request_queue_wait_ms_p95 > 250ms OR queue_depth_p95 > threshold) for 15 minutes

**Threshold guidance:**
- Prefer queue_wait_ms (most interpretable). Default: 250ms p95 for 15 minutes.
- If only queue depth is available, set threshold per model family based on baseline throughput (see dashboard spec). Suggested starting point: queue_depth_p95 > 2 * batch_size_target for 15 minutes.

**Routing:**
- Page: SRE on-call
- Notify: Customer Success escalation channel if account is marked “enterprise_sla=true”

**Why page:** Even though max-bound hit is “expected,” sustained queueing usually indicates one of:
- Customer max is too low relative to demand (needs CS engagement)
- Predictive mode under-provisioned leading into peak
- Provisioning lag/allocator issues preventing scale-up to the max

---

### P1 Paging: Autoscaler stuck (desired != provisioned for too long)
**Condition:** bounded_desired_replicas - provisioned_replicas >= 2 for 20 minutes AND saturation signals indicate load (queue/latency elevated)

**Routing:**
- Page: Infra on-call + SRE on-call

**Notes:**
- This catches provisioning deadlocks and “requested but not placed” failure modes.

---

### P2 Ticket/Slack: Forecast pipeline stale (predictive mode)
**Condition:** predictive_enabled = true AND forecast_staleness_seconds > 900 for 30 minutes

**Routing:**
- Create ticket to Fleet/Infrastructure (autoscaling) + Observability if metrics missing
- Post to #eng-infra (non-paging)

**Notes:**
- Predictive mode must fall back to reactive; paging is only warranted if performance is impacted (covered by queue/latency alerts).

  "text": "[Document context]
Title: ADR-047: Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds — Precedence and Safety Invariants
Source: EnterpriseRAG/confluence
Path: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-autoscaling-bounds-precedence-and-safety-invariants.json
Connector: confluence
Workspace: architecture-and-standards

associated reason

Metric naming and label limits MUST follow the observability standard referenced in related pages (avoid unbounded cardinality).

---

## Alternatives considered
### A1. Soft bounds (warnings only)
Rejected. Customer requirement is contractual guardrails; soft bounds do not meet budget-capping and baseline guarantees.

### A2. Predictive overrides reactive (prediction wins)
Rejected. Reactive metrics are required to prevent overload when predictions are wrong; predictive must not force scale-down into saturation.

### A3. Clamp first, then compute predictive/reactive
Rejected. Clamping early hides the platform’s “requested desired” intent and reduces auditability (cannot reason about why latency regressed while max-bound was hit).

### A4. Scale-up uses max(predictive, reactive), scale-down uses reactive only
Not selected as the default. We allow predictive input into scale-down only when it is valid and scale-down safety gates pass; however, the net effect is still conservative due to cooldown and overload blocks.

---

## Consequences
### Positive
- Customers get deterministic, enforceable behavior aligned with contracts.
- Support and SRE can quickly diagnose “we hit max” vs “prediction stale” vs “region shortage.”
- Predictive scaling can improve p95 latency during known ramps while maintaining safety.

### Tradeoffs / risks
- Customers can misconfigure bounds (e.g., min too high), increasing shortage risk.
- Hard max may cap performance during unexpected spikes (intentional by contract); requires clear UX and CS guidance.
- Conservative scale-down may increase cost slightly vs aggressive reactive downscaling.

---

## Rollout and compatibility notes
- Existing Dedicated deployments retain current behavior until the feature flag is enabled.
- On enablement, defaults must preserve behavior unless customer explicitly sets bounds.
- During pilot, require SRE readiness review and alert tuning before expanding to additional accounts.

  "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Predictive scaling window desync causes reserved-pool shortfalls and customer 5xxs\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-777345-predictive-scale-window-desync-customer-facing.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: engineering\nProject: Dedicated Capacity Stability\nTeam: engineering\n\n3) Observe autoscaler telemetry: controller predicts required headroom but allocator's decay reduces effective headroom quickly; pool size fails to increase fast enough leading to allocation rejections and 5xx gateway errors.\n  - 4) Reproduce across two regions to validate cross-region policy interactions.\n\nCustomer Impact: high\n\nImpact Summary: Multiple enterprise customers experienced degraded availability during morning peak windows for ~2 hours across two regions. Error rates spiked to 6-8% for affected routes and some customers reported production incidents. Business impact includes SLA breaches for higher-tier customers and an open escalation with NimbusPay SRE team.\n\nRoot Cause Summary: The predictive autoscaler (controller) and pool allocator use different smoothing/decay implementations and window alignment. Controller forecasts over a 60s lookahead using exponential smoothing with alpha=0.25 anchored on wall-clock buckets; allocator applies a separate decay factor and a 90s effective smoothing that trims recently observed surge signal earlier than the controller expected. During short, high-amplitude bursts the allocator's aggressive decay caused available headroom to be lower than the controller's planned allocation, leading to delayed or insufficient scale-ups. Edge condition: burst-credit accounting also misaligned by one evaluation tick, allowing bursts to exceed intended limits for a few seconds which downstreamed into allocation churn.\n\nMitigation: Short-term: rolled out a cluster-level feature flag disabling allocator aggressive decay for affected regions and applied a conservative safety buffer (+15% headroom) to predictive allocations for enterprise-tier tenants. Communications: notified impacted customers with NRT incident updates and offered 1:1 postmortem. Medium-term: align smoothing windows and source-of-truth for burst-credit consumption between controller and allocator and add a fast-path preemptive scale-up for >2x baseline sustained >30s.\n\n## Timeline",

`requested_desired` is the desired replica count computed prior to bounds enforcement.
- `bounded_desired` is the desired replica count after applying hard bounds.

### D2. Precedence order for computing requested_desired
The autoscaler computes `requested_desired` using the following precedence and arbitration rules:

1) **Hard safety overrides (scale-up only)**
   - If reactive overload signals exceed critical thresholds (e.g., sustained queue growth / saturation), autoscaler may request an *immediate* scale-up (subject to `max_replicas`).

2) **Predictive desired (if enabled and valid)**
   - If predictive mode is enabled and the forecast is “valid” (fresh, confidence >= minimum, model coverage OK), compute a predictive desired target.

3) **Reactive desired (always available)**
   - Compute reactive desired from observed metrics (queue depth, utilization/saturation, latency signals) using the standard control loop.

4) **Arbitration between predictive and reactive**
   - Requested desired is the **max()** of predictive and reactive desired for scale-up decisions.
   - For scale-down decisions, requested desired is the **min()** of predictive and reactive desired, *subject to scale-down safety rules in D4*.

Rationale: predictive is intended to avoid under-provisioning during ramps, but reactive must still prevent overload if predictions are wrong. For scale-down, we are conservative to prevent churn and under-provisioning.

### D3. Platform defaults do not override explicit customer bounds
Platform defaults (e.g., recommended min, recommended max, default cooldowns) are used only when the customer has not set an explicit value.

Effective policy fields:
- If customer specifies `min_replicas`, it replaces the platform default min.
- If customer specifies `max_replicas`, it replaces the platform default max.
- If a field is unset, platform default applies.

Console MUST display both:
- Customer-configured values (explicit)
- Platform recommended range (informational only)",

Body: Context and intent:
This doc sketches a complementary approach to existing dedicated-capacity autoscaling work: instead of reacting purely to instantaneous load or simple rate-based headroom, use short-horizon demand trajectories to proactively warm compute and KV-cache state, and coordinate graceful evacuation when capacity must be reclaimed. Purpose is operational predictability + fewer cold-token penalties during bursts, while preserving tenant isolation guarantees.

Problem statement (why this is needed):
- Ramp-ups cause token-level latency spikes: cold KV caches + kernel scheduling penalties.
- Traditional warm pools (static or predictive) are either too coarse (wastes capacity) or too slow (misses bursts).
- During forced preemption (eviction, spot reclaim) naive eviction causes large-scale latency/regression for affected tenants.
- Existing approaches handle autoscale and warm pools, but not an integrated trajectory-driven warmup + structured evacuation protocol that respects isolation tags and SLA windows.",

  "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Concurrency Governor: Hybrid Scaling Algorithm & Safety Limits for Dedicated Fleets\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-77421-concurrency-governor-scaling-limiter.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: engineering\nProject: Dedicated Capacity - Autoscaling\nTeam: engineering\n\nobserved concurrency and latency, and a saturating rate limiter that caps scale-up and scale-down velocity. The governor exposes tunable knobs: concurrency_target, headroom_multiplier, max_surge_ratio, min_capacity_floor, and cooldown_window. Runtime will emit debug traces for decisions and contribute to the Console rollouts dashboard.\n\nAlgorithm Details: - Inputs: arrival_rate (requests/sec), observed_concurrency, avg_token_time, KV_cache_hit_ratio, per-tenant reserved_capacity.\n- Predictive estimator: 30s EWMA on arrival_rate and short linear extrapolation to estimate 60s demand.\n- Reactive controller: error = target_concurrency - observed_concurrency; output delta_capacity = Kp*error + Ki*integral(error) (bounded).\n- Velocity limiter: enforce max_scale_up = floor(current_capacity * max_surge_ratio) and max_scale_down = floor(current_capacity * (1 - min_capacity_floor)).\n- Fallbacks: if GPU queue depth > threshold for >30s, route to burst pool if allowed; else trigger paired throttling policy.\n- Configuration: default concurrency_target derived from tenant SLA and model sequence length distribution.\n\nSafety Limits: - Hard caps: max_surge_ratio default 1.25 (25% instantaneous surge), absolute max 2.0 only for flagged enterprise tenants.\n- Min capacity floor: 60% of reserved commit to prevent deep undershoots.\n- Cooldown window: 45s minimum between successive scale adjustments for same pool.\n- Oscillation detector: if >3 direction changes in 5 minutes, halve control gains and emit incident for SRE review.\n- Cost guard: track estimated token spend per minute; if projected 10-minute spend exceeds budget threshold, governor reduces non-critical tenants by proportion until under budget.",

- Base policy: maintain at least 10% headroom over 7-day rolling p75 demand (helps absorb small fluctuations)
- Spike policy: allow burst up to +50% of committed when cluster average latency < target and we have <60% spot utilization
- Cooldown: prefer scale-down cooldown = 8 minutes to avoid oscillation; if we see repeated oscillation, turn on 15m cooldown for that pool

### P1 Paging: Sustained queue buildup while max-bound hit
**Condition:** max_bound_hit = true AND (request_queue_wait_ms_p95 > 250ms OR queue_depth_p95 > threshold) for 15 minutes

result.text:
[Document context]
Title: ADR-047: Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds — Precedence and Safety Invariants
Source: EnterpriseRAG/confluence
Path: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-autoscaling-bounds-precedence-and-safety-invariants.json
Connector: confluence
Workspace: architecture-and-standards

associated reason

Metric naming and label limits MUST follow the observability standard referenced in related pages (avoid unbounded cardinality).

---

## Alternatives considered
### A1. Soft bounds (warnings only)
Rejected. Customer requirement is contractual guardrails; soft bounds do not meet budget-capping and baseline guarantees.

### A2. Predictive overrides reactive (prediction wins)
Rejected. Reactive metrics are required to prevent overload when predictions are wrong; predictive must not force scale-down into saturation.

### A3. Clamp first, then compute predictive/reactive
Rejected. Clamping early hides the platform’s “requested desired” intent and reduces auditability (cannot reason about why latency regressed while max-bound was hit).

### A4. Scale-up uses max(predictive, reactive), scale-down uses reactive only
Not selected as the default. We allow predictive input into scale-down only when it is valid and scale-down safety gates pass; however, the net effect is still conservative due to cooldown and overload blocks.

---

## Consequences
### Positive
- Customers get deterministic, enforceable behavior aligned with contracts.
- Support and SRE can quickly diagnose “we hit max” vs “prediction stale” vs “region shortage.”
- Predictive scaling can improve p95 latency during known ramps while maintaining safety.

### Tradeoffs / risks
- Customers can misconfigure bounds (e.g., min too high), increasing shortage risk.
- Hard max may cap performance during unexpected spikes (intentional by contract); requires clear UX and CS guidance.
- Conservative scale-down may increase cost slightly vs aggressive reactive downscaling.

---

## Rollout and compatibility notes
- Existing Dedicated deployments retain current behavior until the feature flag is enabled.
- On enablement, defaults must preserve behavior unless customer explicitly sets bounds.
- During pilot, require SRE readiness review and alert tuning before expanding to additional accounts.

---

Source: EnterpriseRAG/linear

Connector: linear
Workspace: engineering
Project: Dedicated Capacity Stability
Team: engineering

3) Observe autoscaler telemetry: controller predicts required headroom but allocator's decay reduces effective headroom quickly; pool size fails to increase fast enough leading to allocation rejections and 5xx gateway errors.
  - 4) Reproduce across two regions to validate cross-region policy interactions.

Customer Impact: high

Impact Summary: Multiple enterprise customers experienced degraded availability during morning peak windows for ~2 hours across two regions. Error rates spiked to 6-8% for affected routes and some customers reported production incidents. Business impact includes SLA breaches for higher-tier customers and an open escalation with NimbusPay SRE team.

Root Cause Summary: The predictive autoscaler (controller) and pool allocator use different smoothing/decay implementations and window alignment. Controller forecasts over a 60s lookahead using exponential smoothing with alpha=0.25 anchored on wall-clock buckets; allocator applies a separate decay factor and a 90s effective smoothing that trims recently observed surge signal earlier than the controller expected. During short, high-amplitude bursts the allocator's aggressive decay caused available headroom to be lower than the controller's planned allocation, leading to delayed or insufficient scale-ups. Edge condition: burst-credit accounting also misaligned by one evaluation tick, allowing bursts to exceed intended limits for a few seconds which downstreamed into allocation churn.

Mitigation: Short-term: rolled out a cluster-level feature flag disabling allocator aggressive decay for affected regions and applied a conservative safety buffer (+15% headroom) to predictive allocations for enterprise-tier tenants. Communications: notified impacted customers with NRT incident updates and offered 1:1 postmortem. Medium-term: align smoothing windows and source-of-truth for burst-credit consumption between controller and allocator and add a fast-path preemptive scale-up for >2x baseline sustained >30s.

## Timeline

result.text:
[Document context]

Source: EnterpriseRAG/confluence

Connector: confluence
Workspace: architecture-and-standards

`requested_desired` is the desired replica count computed prior to bounds enforcement.
- `bounded_desired` is the desired replica count after applying hard bounds.

### D2. Precedence order for computing requested_desired
The autoscaler computes `requested_desired` using the following precedence and arbitration rules:

1) **Hard safety overrides (scale-up only)**
   - If reactive overload signals exceed critical thresholds (e.g., sustained queue growth / saturation), autoscaler may request an *immediate* scale-up (subject to `max_replicas`).

2) **Predictive desired (if enabled and valid)**
   - If predictive mode is enabled and the forecast is “valid” (fresh, confidence >= minimum, model coverage OK), compute a predictive desired target.

3) **Reactive desired (always available)**
   - Compute reactive desired from observed metrics (queue depth, utilization/saturation, latency signals) using the standard control loop.

4) **Arbitration between predictive and reactive**
   - Requested desired is the **max()** of predictive and reactive desired for scale-up decisions.
   - For scale-down decisions, requested desired is the **min()** of predictive and reactive desired, *subject to scale-down safety rules in D4*.

Rationale: predictive is intended to avoid under-provisioning during ramps, but reactive must still prevent overload if predictions are wrong. For scale-down, we are conservative to prevent churn and under-provisioning.

### D3. Platform defaults do not override explicit customer bounds
Platform defaults (e.g., recommended min, recommended max, default cooldowns) are used only when the customer has not set an explicit value.

Effective policy fields:
- If customer specifies `min_replicas`, it replaces the platform default min.
- If customer specifies `max_replicas`, it replaces the platform default max.
- If a field is unset, platform default applies.

Console MUST display both:
- Customer-configured values (explicit)
- Platform recommended range (informational only)

Body: Context and intent:
This doc sketches a complementary approach to existing dedicated-capacity autoscaling work: instead of reacting purely to instantaneous load or simple rate-based headroom, use short-horizon demand trajectories to proactively warm compute and KV-cache state, and coordinate graceful evacuation when capacity must be reclaimed. Purpose is operational predictability + fewer cold-token penalties during bursts, while preserving tenant isolation guarantees.

Problem statement (why this is needed):
- Ramp-ups cause token-level latency spikes: cold KV caches + kernel scheduling penalties.
- Traditional warm pools (static or predictive) are either too coarse (wastes capacity) or too slow (misses bursts).
- During forced preemption (eviction, spot reclaim) naive eviction causes large-scale latency/regression for affected tenants.
- Existing approaches handle autoscale and warm pools, but not an integrated trajectory-driven warmup + structured evacuation protocol that respects isolation tags and SLA windows.

observed concurrency and latency, and a saturating rate limiter that caps scale-up and scale-down velocity. The governor exposes tunable knobs: concurrency_target, headroom_multiplier, max_surge_ratio, min_capacity_floor, and cooldown_window. Runtime will emit debug traces for decisions and contribute to the Console rollouts dashboard.

Algorithm Details: - Inputs: arrival_rate (requests/sec), observed_concurrency, avg_token_time, KV_cache_hit_ratio, per-tenant reserved_capacity.
- Predictive estimator: 30s EWMA on arrival_rate and short linear extrapolation to estimate 60s demand.
- Reactive controller: error = target_concurrency - observed_concurrency; output delta_capacity = Kp*error + Ki*integral(error) (bounded).
- Velocity limiter: enforce max_scale_up = floor(current_capacity * max_surge_ratio) and max_scale_down = floor(current_capacity * (1 - min_capacity_floor)).
- Fallbacks: if GPU queue depth > threshold for >30s, route to burst pool if allowed; else trigger paired throttling policy.
- Configuration: default concurrency_target derived from tenant SLA and model sequence length distribution.

Safety Limits: - Hard caps: max_surge_ratio default 1.25 (25% instantaneous surge), absolute max 2.0 only for flagged enterprise tenants.
- Min capacity floor: 60% of reserved commit to prevent deep undershoots.
- Cooldown window: 45s minimum between successive scale adjustments for same pool.
- Oscillation detector: if >3 direction changes in 5 minutes, halve control gains and emit incident for SRE review.
- Cost guard: track estimated token spend per minute; if projected 10-minute spend exceeds budget threshold, governor reduces non-critical tenants by proportion until under budget.

(i.e., 50 GPU shortfall during peaks)
- Spike profile: median spike duration ~22 minutes, 95th percentile spike ~2.1 hours
- Cost: spot/burst instance effective cost ~ $1.45 / GPU-hour; reserved committed amortized cost ~ $0.95 / GPU-hour

Simple forecast assumptions (for discussion):
- Traffic growth: 12% MoM (observed product triggers and new customer onboardings)
- If growth holds, p95 demand in 8 weeks -> ~ 210 * 1.12^2 ~= 263 GPUs
- Option A (conservative): ramp reservations to 220 GPUs over next 6 weeks (+60 GPUs) and rely on burst for remaining peaks
- Option B (cost-forward): keep reservations at 160, increase burst capacity and tighten autoscale latency SLOs to ensure cold-start < 30s; risk = cost volatility + potential transient throttles

Operational constraints / notes:
- Procurement lead time for dedicated reservations: ~3-4 weeks for contract + provisioning
- Dedicated SLA requires 99.9% availability for reserved pool; autoscale nodes are best-effort and do not count for reserved SLA
- Caching and batching improvements expected to reduce token-level cost by ~7% if we deploy prefix-KV tuning in next sprint

Autoscale policy ideas (draft):
- Base policy: maintain at least 10% headroom over 7-day rolling p75 demand (helps absorb small fluctuations)
- Spike policy: allow burst up to +50% of committed when cluster average latency < target and we have <60% spot utilization
- Cooldown: prefer scale-down cooldown = 8 minutes to avoid oscillation; if we see repeated oscillation, turn on 15m cooldown for that pool
- Pre-warm option: for predictable large night jobs, schedule pre-warm instances at T-20m for large batch runs

Controller design (high level):
- Runtime controller: A lightweight agent colocated with the serving shard. Maintains a sliding window of request signals, applies conservative heuristics to make fast, reversible adjustments (aim for sub-1s decision latency). Only applies adjustments that map to pre-certified fidelity profiles.
- Calibration decision service: A control-plane service that consumes aggregated telemetry, runs predictive models (time-series forecasting of latency and cost under candidate profiles) and recommends parameterized policies. It also stores the audit log for every adjustment and computes impact estimates used in rollout decisions.

Calibration algorithm summary:
1) Observe recent signals (latency, cost, shadow-eval quality).
2) Predict short-term latency/cost under each candidate profile using an ensemble: (a) linear transfer function tuned per-model and per-sequence-length, (b) small amortized ML model trained on historical traces.
3) Score candidates with a loss that weights latency-SLO violations and quality delta (default: latency weight 0.6, quality weight 0.4).
4) Select lowest-loss candidate that is allowed by policy and that has been certified for this tenant.
5) Apply adjustment with a conservative ramp: 10% of traffic -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% over 15 minutes subject to fast rollback triggers.",

  "title": "Concurrency Governor: Hybrid Scaling Algorithm & Safety Limits for Dedicated Fleets",
  "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Concurrency Governor: Hybrid Scaling Algorithm & Safety Limits for Dedicated Fleets\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-77421-concurrency-governor-scaling-limiter.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: engineering\nProject: Dedicated Capacity - Autoscaling\nTeam: engineering\n\nobserved concurrency and latency, and a saturating rate limiter that caps scale-up and scale-down velocity. The governor exposes tunable knobs: concurrency_target, headroom_multiplier, max_surge_ratio, min_capacity_floor, and cooldown_window. Runtime will emit debug traces for decisions and contribute to the Console rollouts dashboard.\n\nAlgorithm Details: - Inputs: arrival_rate (requests/sec), observed_concurrency, avg_token_time, KV_cache_hit_ratio, per-tenant reserved_capacity.\n- Predictive estimator: 30s EWMA on arrival_rate and short linear extrapolation to estimate 60s demand.\n- Reactive controller: error = target_concurrency - observed_concurrency; output delta_capacity = Kp*error + Ki*integral(error) (bounded).\n- Velocity limiter: enforce max_scale_up = floor(current_capacity * max_surge_ratio) and max_scale_down = floor(current_capacity * (1 - min_capacity_floor)).\n- Fallbacks: if GPU queue depth > threshold for >30s, route to burst pool if allowed; else trigger paired throttling policy.\n- Configuration: default concurrency_target derived from tenant SLA and model sequence length distribution.\n\nSafety Limits: - Hard caps: max_surge_ratio default 1.25 (25% instantaneous surge), absolute max 2.0 only for flagged enterprise tenants.\n- Min capacity floor: 60% of reserved commit to prevent deep undershoots.\n- Cooldown window: 45s minimum between successive scale adjustments for same pool.\n- Oscillation detector: if >3 direction changes in 5 minutes, halve control gains and emit incident for SRE review.\n- Cost guard: track estimated token spend per minute; if projected 10-minute spend exceeds budget threshold, governor reduces non-critical tenants by proportion until under budget.",

cause reactive overprovisioning or missed SLOs before scaling completes, and (2) cost-inefficient oscillations when traffic rapidly changes. Several related tickets implemented safety envelopes and conservative stepping, but none incorporate predictive headroom. Customer complaints from three enterprise Dedicated tenants noted latency regressions during predictable marketing spikes.

Proposed Solution: Build a lightweight forecasting module (exponential smoothing + seasonality detector) in the autoscaler service to predict 1-30min horizon throughput and tail latency proxies. Compute a headroom target: predicted_peak * safety_margin + min_capacity. Use an adaptive controller that translates headroom delta into scale actions with a PI-inspired controller, but capped by per-tenant hard limits and global fleet safety windows. Integrate a circuit-breaker that prevents scaling above emergency ceiling unless sustained over 2 minutes. Provide knobs: forecast_horizon, safety_margin_pct, max_step_percent, cooldown_s, and emergency_ceiling. Expose metrics and a dashboard and add canary rollout to 5% of Dedicated clusters.

## Decisions

- Use single-model ETS (error-trend-seasonality) style forecasting implemented in Go for low latency and deterministic resource use
  - Forecast horizons: default 5 minutes; configurable up to 30 minutes per project
  - Controller algorithm: PI-inspired mapping of headroom delta to steps with exponential backoff on repeated failures
  - Safety limits: per-tenant floor/ceiling plus a cross-tenant emergency ceiling enforced by fleet controller
  - Circuit-breaker triggers require predicted headroom > emergency_ceiling OR observed sustained p95 breach for >120s
  - No immediate autoscale-down on short negative forecast spikes: require sustained 3x check intervals before reduction

## Tradeoffs

## Tradeoffs

- Forecasting reduces missed SLOs for predictable patterns but introduces risk if model overestimates — mitigated by hard emergency ceilings

Controller design (high level):
- Runtime controller: A lightweight agent colocated with the serving shard. Maintains a sliding window of request signals, applies conservative heuristics to make fast, reversible adjustments (aim for sub-1s decision latency). Only applies adjustments that map to pre-certified fidelity profiles.
- Calibration decision service: A control-plane service that consumes aggregated telemetry, runs predictive models (time-series forecasting of latency and cost under candidate profiles) and recommends parameterized policies. It also stores the audit log for every adjustment and computes impact estimates used in rollout decisions.

Calibration algorithm summary:
1) Observe recent signals (latency, cost, shadow-eval quality).
2) Predict short-term latency/cost under each candidate profile using an ensemble: (a) linear transfer function tuned per-model and per-sequence-length, (b) small amortized ML model trained on historical traces.
3) Score candidates with a loss that weights latency-SLO violations and quality delta (default: latency weight 0.6, quality weight 0.4).
4) Select lowest-loss candidate that is allowed by policy and that has been certified for this tenant.
5) Apply adjustment with a conservative ramp: 10% of traffic -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% over 15 minutes subject to fast rollback triggers.

observed concurrency and latency, and a saturating rate limiter that caps scale-up and scale-down velocity. The governor exposes tunable knobs: concurrency_target, headroom_multiplier, max_surge_ratio, min_capacity_floor, and cooldown_window. Runtime will emit debug traces for decisions and contribute to the Console rollouts dashboard.

Algorithm Details: - Inputs: arrival_rate (requests/sec), observed_concurrency, avg_token_time, KV_cache_hit_ratio, per-tenant reserved_capacity.
- Predictive estimator: 30s EWMA on arrival_rate and short linear extrapolation to estimate 60s demand.
- Reactive controller: error = target_concurrency - observed_concurrency; output delta_capacity = Kp*error + Ki*integral(error) (bounded).
- Velocity limiter: enforce max_scale_up = floor(current_capacity * max_surge_ratio) and max_scale_down = floor(current_capacity * (1 - min_capacity_floor)).
- Fallbacks: if GPU queue depth > threshold for >30s, route to burst pool if allowed; else trigger paired throttling policy.
- Configuration: default concurrency_target derived from tenant SLA and model sequence length distribution.

Safety Limits: - Hard caps: max_surge_ratio default 1.25 (25% instantaneous surge), absolute max 2.0 only for flagged enterprise tenants.
- Min capacity floor: 60% of reserved commit to prevent deep undershoots.
- Cooldown window: 45s minimum between successive scale adjustments for same pool.
- Oscillation detector: if >3 direction changes in 5 minutes, halve control gains and emit incident for SRE review.
- Cost guard: track estimated token spend per minute; if projected 10-minute spend exceeds budget threshold, governor reduces non-critical tenants by proportion until under budget.

Description: Summary: We need a predictive headroom projection module and an accompanying tiered memory-budgeting policy that dynamically apportions GPU memory across model weights, KV cache, and activations for mixed-priority inference workloads. The goal is to reduce OOMs and tail-latency spikes while preserving throughput and lowering token cost via better continuous batching and preemptive eviction signals.\n\nProblem details: Current heuristics allocate fixed soft quotas for weights/KV/activations and rely on reactive eviction once pressure is high. The policy exposes a graded eviction cascade and preemption signals to the continuous-batcher. 4) Integrate with the runtime advisor to allow short-term optimistic batching decisions when projected headroom exceeds a safety margin. 5) Provide runtime knobs and telemetry: quantile target, projection horizon, conservative multiplier, model-priority maps.\n\nDesign constraints and trade-offs: - Keep PHE op-cost low: must run in <1ms per GPU per projection window and avoid adding heavy centralized coordination. - Conservative defaults for enterprise tenants (lower quantile target). - Prefer amortized compression over sync host spill for latency-sensitive

    "content": "{\n  \"key\": \"ENG-62670\",\n  \"team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"title\": \"Workload-forecast-based headroom controller for Dedicated capacity\",\n  \"status\": \"In Progress\",\n  \"priority\": \"P0\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-02-20\",\n  \"updated_at\": \"2026-03-10\",\n  \"creator\": \"Asha Patel\",\n  \"assignee\": \"Miguel Torres\",\n  \"project\": \"Dedicated-Autoscale-Next\",\n  \"cycle\": \"2026-W09\",\n  \"estimate\": \"8\",\n  \"due_date\": \"2026-03-31\",\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"autoscaling\",\n    \"dedicated\",\n    \"throughput\",\n    \"safety\",\n    \"forecasting\"\n  ],\n  \"description\": \"Introduce a headroom controller that uses short-horizon workload forecasts to proactively provision and maintain throughput guarantees for Dedicated capacity. The controller combines forecasting, conservative step sizing, and circuit-breaker safety limits to reduce SLA violations and avoid oscillatory scale behavior during traffic spikes and diurnal patterns.\",\n  \"background\": \"Current autoscaler reacts to observed metrics (p95 latency, tokens/sec) and applies conservative steps with cooldowns. We observe two issues: (1) transient spikes cause reactive overprovisioning or missed SLOs before scaling completes, and (2) cost-inefficient oscillations when traffic rapidly changes. Several related tickets implemented safety envelopes and conservative stepping, but none incorporate predictive headroom. Customer complaints from three enterprise Dedicated tenants noted latency regressions during predictable marketing spikes.\",\n  \"proposed_solution\": \"Build a lightweight forecasting module (exponential smoothing + seasonality detector) in the autoscaler service to predict 1-30min horizon throughput and tail latency proxies. Compute a headroom target: predicted_peak * safety_margin + min_capacity. Use an adaptive controller that translates headroom delta into scale actions with a PI-inspired controller, but capped by per-tenant hard limits and global fleet safety windows. Integrate a circuit-breaker that prevents scaling above emergency ceiling unless sustained over 2 minutes. Provide knobs: forecast_horizon, safety_margin_pct, max_step_percent, cooldown_s, and emergency_ceiling. Expose metrics and a dashboard and add canary rollout to 5% of Dedicated clusters.\",\n  \"decisions\": [\n    \"Use single-model ETS (error-trend-seasonality) style forecasting implemented in Go for low latency and deterministic resource use\",\n    \"Forecast horizons: default 5 minutes; configurable up to 30 minutes per project\",\n    \"Controller algorithm: PI-inspired mapping of headroom delta to steps with exponential backoff on repeated failures\",\n    \"Safety limits: per-tenant floor/ceiling plus a cross-tenant emergency ceiling enforced by fleet controller\",\n    \"Circuit-breaker triggers require predicted headroom > emergency_ceiling OR observed sustained p95 breach for >120s\",\n    \"No immediate autoscale-down on short negative forecast spikes: require sustained 3x check intervals before reduction\"\n  ],\n  \"tradeoffs\": [\n    \"Forecasting reduces missed SLOs for predictable patterns but introduces risk if model overestimates \\u2014 mitigated by hard emergency ceilings\",\n    \"Adding forecasting increases autoscaler complexity and CPU usage; we chose simple ETS to minimize compute and maintenance burden\",\n    \"Longer forecast horizons improve anticipation but increase false positives; default is conservative (5m) and configurable\",\n    \"PI-style controller is easier to reason about than full RL or optimization but may be suboptimal for complex multi-tenant interactions\",\n    \"Canary rollout and strict safety limits increase deployment time but are necessary to prevent fleet-wide regressions\"\n  ],\n  \"tasks\": [\n    \"Design forecasting API and storage for short-term series (in-memory ring buffer + optional TS write) - Miguel\",\n    \"Implement ETS forecasting module in autoscaler core - Miguel\",\n    \"Implement headroom-to-step mapping and PI-inspired controller - Miguel\",\n    \"Add per-tenant safety envelope enforcement and emergency ceiling in fleet orchestrator - Backend team\",\n    \"Unit + integration tests for forecast accuracy, step sizing boundaries, and circuit-breaker behavior - QA\",\n    \"Dashboard and alerting (predicted_peak, headroom, scale_decisions, circuit_breaker_events) - Observability\",\n    \"Confluence design doc and rollout runbook - Asha\",\n    \"Canary rollout to 5% of clusters and monitor SLOs for 72 hours - SRE\"\n  ],\n  \"comments\": [\n    \"2026-02-21 Miguel: spike analysis shows marketing events are highly seasonal; simple ETS yields 78% improvement in 5m peak prediction vs naive mean.\",\n    \"2026-02-28 Asha: design doc posted https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/DED/Forecast-Headroom-Controller; please add review comments there.\",\n    \"2026-03-03 PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/autoscaler/pull/493 - initial ETS + controller impl\",\n    \"2026-03-05 Design review (PM+SRE): agreed on 5m default horizon, emergency_ceiling default set to 2x committed capacity\",\n    \"2026-03-08 QA: found an edge case when forecasting with zero-warmup series \\u2014 added warm-start fallback to short moving-average\",\n    \"2026-03-10 SRE: canary runbook uploaded https://runbooks.redwood.ai/dedicated-autoscale-canary; slated for 2026-03-18 start\"\n  ],\n  \"acceptance_criteria\": [\n    \"Autoscaler can produce 5m and 15m forecasts with documented error bounds in test harness\",\n    \"Headroom controller produces deterministic scale_up/scale_down actions given synthetic traces and obeys safety envelopes\",\n    \"No regression in median latency for non-canary clusters during canary rollout (SLO: p95 < committed_slo + 5%)\",\n    \"Dashboard surfaces predicted_peak, headroom, controller_decision_reason, and circuit_breaker_events\",\n    \"Runbook exists and automated rollback triggers if SLOs worsen beyond threshold during canary\"\n  ],\n  \"dependencies\": [\n    \"ENG-48123\",\n    \"ENG-35602\",\n    \"ENG-27514\"\n  ],\n  \"release\": \"dedicated-2026.04\",\n  \"customer_impact\": \"high\",\n  \"security_review_required\": \"false\",\n  \"parent_issue\": [\n    \"ENG-50246\"\n  ],\n  \"original_location\": \"linear/engineering/ENG-62670-workload-forecast-headroom-controller.json\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"description\",\n    \"background\",\n    \"proposed_solution\",\n    \"decisions\",\n    \"tradeoffs\",\n    \"tasks\",\n    \"comments\",\n    \"acceptance_criteria\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_d921e1d4282b45a7b4990e2366bedc05\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Workload-forecast-based headroom controller for Dedicated capacity\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/business-ops/ENG-62670-workload-forecast-headroom-controller.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: business-ops\nProject: Dedicated-Autoscale-Next\nTeam: engineering\n\ncause reactive overprovisioning or missed SLOs before scaling completes, and (2) cost-inefficient oscillations when traffic rapidly changes. Several related tickets implemented safety envelopes and conservative stepping, but none incorporate predictive headroom. Customer complaints from three enterprise Dedicated tenants noted latency regressions during predictable marketing spikes.\n\nProposed Solution: Build a lightweight forecasting module (exponential smoothing + seasonality detector) in the autoscaler service to predict 1-30min horizon throughput and tail latency proxies. Compute a headroom target: predicted_peak * safety_margin + min_capacity. Use an adaptive controller that translates headroom delta into scale actions with a PI-inspired controller, but capped by per-tenant hard limits and global fleet safety windows. Integrate a circuit-breaker that prevents scaling above emergency ceiling unless sustained over 2 minutes. Provide knobs: forecast_horizon, safety_margin_pct, max_step_percent, cooldown_s, and emergency_ceiling. Expose metrics and a dashboard and add canary rollout to 5% of Dedicated clusters.\n\n## Decisions\n\n- Use single-model ETS (error-trend-seasonality) style forecasting implemented in Go for low latency and deterministic resource use\n  - Forecast horizons: default 5 minutes; configurable up to 30 minutes per project\n  - Controller algorithm: PI-inspired mapping of headroom delta to steps with exponential backoff on repeated failures\n  - Safety limits: per-tenant floor/ceiling plus a cross-tenant emergency ceiling enforced by fleet controller\n  - Circuit-breaker triggers require predicted headroom > emergency_ceiling OR observed sustained p95 breach for >120s\n  - No immediate autoscale-down on short negative forecast spikes: require sustained 3x check intervals before reduction\n\n## Tradeoffs",
