      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Workload-forecast-based headroom controller for Dedicated capacity\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/business-ops/ENG-62670-workload-forecast-headroom-controller.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: business-ops\nProject: Dedicated-Autoscale-Next\nTeam: engineering\n\niling plus a cross-tenant emergency ceiling enforced by fleet controller\n  - Circuit-breaker triggers require predicted headroom > emergency_ceiling OR observed sustained p95 breach for >120s\n  - No immediate autoscale-down on short negative forecast spikes: require sustained 3x check intervals before reduction\n\n## Tradeoffs\n\n- Forecasting reduces missed SLOs for predictable patterns but introduces risk if model overestimates — mitigated by hard emergency ceilings\n  - Adding forecasting increases autoscaler complexity and CPU usage; we chose simple ETS to minimize compute and maintenance burden\n  - Longer forecast horizons improve anticipation but increase false positives; default is conservative (5m) and configurable\n  - PI-style controller is easier to reason about than full RL or optimization but may be suboptimal for complex multi-tenant interactions\n  - Canary rollout and strict safety limits increase deployment time but are necessary to prevent fleet-wide regressions\n\n## Tasks\n\n- Design forecasting API and storage for short-term series (in-memory ring buffer + optional TS write) - Miguel\n  - Implement ETS forecasting module in autoscaler core - Miguel\n  - Implement headroom-to-step mapping and PI-inspired controller - Miguel\n  - Add per-tenant safety envelope enforcement and emergency ceiling in fleet orchestrator - Backend team\n  - Unit + integration tests for forecast accuracy, step sizing boundaries, and circuit-breaker behavior - QA\n  - Dashboard and alerting (predicted_peak, headroom, scale_decisions, circuit_breaker_events) - Observability\n  - Confluence design doc and rollout runbook - Asha\n  - Canary rollout to 5% of clusters and monitor SLOs for 72 hours - SRE\n\n## Comments",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Workload-forecast-based headroom controller for Dedicated capacity\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/business-ops/ENG-62670-workload-forecast-headroom-controller.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: business-ops\nProject: Dedicated-Autoscale-Next\nTeam: engineering\n\n- Dashboard and alerting (predicted_peak, headroom, scale_decisions, circuit_breaker_events) - Observability\n  - Confluence design doc and rollout runbook - Asha\n  - Canary rollout to 5% of clusters and monitor SLOs for 72 hours - SRE\n\n## Comments\n\n- 2026-02-21 Miguel: spike analysis shows marketing events are highly seasonal; simple ETS yields 78% improvement in 5m peak prediction vs naive mean.\n  - 2026-02-28 Asha: design doc posted https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/DED/Forecast-Headroom-Controller; please add review comments there.\n  - 2026-03-03 PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/autoscaler/pull/493 - initial ETS + controller impl\n  - 2026-03-05 Design review (PM+SRE): agreed on 5m default horizon, emergency_ceiling default set to 2x committed capacity\n  - 2026-03-08 QA: found an edge case when forecasting with zero-warmup series — added warm-start fallback to short moving-average\n  - 2026-03-10 SRE: canary runbook uploaded https://runbooks.redwood.ai/dedicated-autoscale-canary; slated for 2026-03-18 start\n\n## Acceptance Criteria\n\n- Autoscaler can produce 5m and 15m forecasts with documented error bounds in test harness\n  - Headroom controller produces deterministic scale_up/scale_down actions given synthetic traces and obeys safety envelopes\n  - No regression in median latency for non-canary clusters during canary rollout (SLO: p95 < committed_slo + 5%)\n  - Dashboard surfaces predicted_peak, headroom, controller_decision_reason, and circuit_breaker_events\n  - Runbook exists and automated rollback triggers if SLOs worsen beyond threshold during canary\n\n## Dependencies\n\n- ENG-48123\n  - ENG-35602\n  - ENG-27514",

# Workload-forecast-based headroom controller for Dedicated capacity

Key: ENG-62670

Team: engineering

Title: Workload-forecast-based headroom controller for Dedicated capacity

Status: In Progress

Priority: P0

Created At: 2026-02-20

Updated At: 2026-03-10

Creator: Asha Patel

Assignee: Miguel Torres

Project: Dedicated-Autoscale-Next

Cycle: 2026-W09

Estimate: 8

Due Date: 2026-03-31

## Labels

- autoscaling
  - dedicated
  - throughput
  - safety
  - forecasting

Description: Introduce a headroom controller that uses short-horizon workload forecasts to proactively provision and maintain throughput guarantees for Dedicated capacity. The controller combines forecasting, conservative step sizing, and circuit-breaker safety limits to reduce SLA violations and avoid oscillatory scale behavior during traffic spikes and diurnal patterns.

Background: Current autoscaler reacts to observed metrics (p95 latency, tokens/sec) and applies conservative steps with cooldowns. We observe two issues: (1) transient spikes cause reactive overprovisioning or missed SLOs before scaling completes, and (2) cost-inefficient oscillations when traffic rapidly changes. Several related tickets implemented safety envelopes and conservative stepping, but none incorporate predictive headroom. Customer complaints from three enterprise Dedicated tenants noted latency regressions during predictable marketing spikes.

Title: Workload-forecast-based headroom controller for Dedicated capacity
Source: EnterpriseRAG/linear
Path: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/business-ops/ENG-62670-workload-forecast-headroom-controller.json
Connector: linear
Workspace: business-ops
Project: Dedicated-Autoscale-Next
Team: engineering

cause reactive overprovisioning or missed SLOs before scaling completes, and (2) cost-inefficient oscillations when traffic rapidly changes. Several related tickets implemented safety envelopes and conservative stepping, but none incorporate predictive headroom. Customer complaints from three enterprise Dedicated tenants noted latency regressions during predictable marketing spikes.

Proposed Solution: Build a lightweight forecasting module (exponential smoothing + seasonality detector) in the autoscaler service to predict 1-30min horizon throughput and tail latency proxies. Compute a headroom target: predicted_peak * safety_margin + min_capacity. Use an adaptive controller that translates headroom delta into scale actions with a PI-inspired controller, but capped by per-tenant hard limits and global fleet safety windows. Integrate a circuit-breaker that prevents scaling above emergency ceiling unless sustained over 2 minutes. Provide knobs: forecast_horizon, safety_margin_pct, max_step_percent, cooldown_s, and emergency_ceiling. Expose metrics and a dashboard and add canary rollout to 5% of Dedicated clusters.

## Decisions

- Use single-model ETS (error-trend-seasonality) style forecasting implemented in Go for low latency and deterministic resource use
  - Forecast horizons: default 5 minutes; configurable up to 30 minutes per project
  - Controller algorithm: PI-inspired mapping of headroom delta to steps with exponential backoff on repeated failures
  - Safety limits: per-tenant floor/ceiling plus a cross-tenant emergency ceiling enforced by fleet controller
  - Circuit-breaker triggers require predicted headroom > emergency_ceiling OR observed sustained p95 breach for >120s
  - No immediate autoscale-down on short negative forecast spikes: require sustained 3x check intervals before reduction

## Tradeoffs

  - Circuit-breaker triggers require predicted headroom > emergency_ceiling OR observed sustained p95 breach for >120s
  - No immediate autoscale-down on short negative forecast spikes: require sustained 3x check intervals before reduction

## Tradeoffs

- Forecasting reduces missed SLOs for predictable patterns but introduces risk if model overestimates — mitigated by hard emergency ceilings
  - Adding forecasting increases autoscaler complexity and CPU usage; we chose simple ETS to minimize compute and maintenance burden
  - Longer forecast horizons improve anticipation but increase false positives; default is conservative (5m) and configurable
  - PI-style controller is easier to reason about than full RL or optimization but may be suboptimal for complex multi-tenant interactions
  - Canary rollout and strict safety limits increase deployment time but are necessary to prevent fleet-wide regressions

  - Canary rollout to 5% of clusters and monitor SLOs for 72 hours - SRE

    "id": "dsid_fa6744f09ed34014a2cb2c8f2fb979f2",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-777345-predictive-scale-window-desync-customer-facing.json",
    "title": "Predictive scaling window desync causes reserved-pool shortfalls and customer 5xxs",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/linear",
    "content": "{\n  \"key\": \"ENG-777345\",\n  \"team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"title\": \"Predictive scaling window desync causes reserved-pool shortfalls and customer 5xxs\",\n  \"status\": \"In Progress\",\n  \"priority\": \"P0\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2025-11-04\",\n  \"updated_at\": \"2025-11-12\",\n  \"creator\": \"Ava Thompson\",\n  \"assignee\": \"Marcus Li\",\n  \"project\": \"Dedicated Capacity Stability\",\n  \"cycle\": \"2025-W44\",\n  \"estimate\": \"8\",\n  \"due_date\": \"2025-11-18\",\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"dedicated\",\n    \"autoscaler\",\n    \"reserved-pool\",\n    \"customer-escalation\",\n    \"high-priority\"\n  ],\n  \"description\": \"Summary: During coordinated morning traffic spikes we observed repeated reserved-pool shortfalls for several enterprise tenants (notably NimbusPay and ArbourRetail) that triggered customer-facing 5xx errors and increased latency. Investigation indicates a desynchronization between the predictive autoscaler windowing logic (controller) and the allocator's traffic smoothing/decay function, which resulted in under-provisioned reserved pools for short, high-amplitude bursts. This ticket tracks the bugfix, mitigations, communications, and follow-up hardening work.\",\n  \"reproduction_steps\": [\n    \"1) Use a dedicated tenant with reserved pool enabled and burst credits configured.\",\n    \"2) Replay a synthetic traffic pattern: 3x baseline QPS for 90s, 1.2x for 10s, then drop to baseline. Repeat on 3-minute cadence.\",\n    \"3) Observe autoscaler telemetry: controller predicts required headroom but allocator's decay reduces effective headroom quickly; pool size fails to increase fast enough leading to allocation rejections and 5xx gateway errors.\",\n    \"4) Reproduce across two regions to validate cross-region policy interactions.\"\n  ],\n  \"customer_impact\": \"high\",\n  \"impact_summary\": \"Multiple enterprise customers experienced degraded availability during morning peak windows for ~2 hours across two regions. Error rates spiked to 6-8% for affected routes and some customers reported production incidents. Business impact includes SLA breaches for higher-tier customers and an open escalation with NimbusPay SRE team.\",\n  \"root_cause_summary\": \"The predictive autoscaler (controller) and pool allocator use different smoothing/decay implementations and window alignment. Controller forecasts over a 60s lookahead using exponential smoothing with alpha=0.25 anchored on wall-clock buckets; allocator applies a separate decay factor and a 90s effective smoothing that trims recently observed surge signal earlier than the controller expected. During short, high-amplitude bursts the allocator's aggressive decay caused available headroom to be lower than the controller's planned allocation, leading to delayed or insufficient scale-ups. Edge condition: burst-credit accounting also misaligned by one evaluation tick, allowing bursts to exceed intended limits for a few seconds which downstreamed into allocation churn.\",\n  \"mitigation\": \"Short-term: rolled out a cluster-level feature flag disabling allocator aggressive decay for affected regions and applied a conservative safety buffer (+15% headroom) to predictive allocations for enterprise-tier tenants. Communications: notified impacted customers with NRT incident updates and offered 1:1 postmortem. Medium-term: align smoothing windows and source-of-truth for burst-credit consumption between controller and allocator and add a fast-path preemptive scale-up for >2x baseline sustained >30s.\",\n  \"timeline\": [\n    \"2025-11-04 06:42 UTC: Pager triggered - spikes observed in us-west-2 for reserved pools. NimbusPay SRE reached out via support channel.\",\n    \"2025-11-04 07:10 UTC: Initial mitigation - enabled safety buffer via runtime config for affected tenants; immediate error rate reduced but not fully resolved.\",\n    \"2025-11-04 09:30 UTC: Root-cause hypothesis formed: smoothing/window mismatch between controller and allocator.\",\n    \"2025-11-05 13:00 UTC: Hotfix PR submitted that aligns decay math to controller's exponential smoothing and adds a one-evaluation tick headroom reserve.\",\n    \"2025-11-06 02:00 UTC: Hotfix deployed to canary clusters in us-west-2 and eu-west-1; observed 90% reduction in allocation rejections.\",\n    \"2025-11-08 21:15 UTC: Stakeholder review: PM and Reliability approved rollout to remaining regions with gradual ramp.\",\n    \"2025-11-12 10:00 UTC: Rollout to all regions in progress; monitoring shows stable headroom for 72h window.\"\n  ],\n  \"linked_PRs\": [\n    \"github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/6421\",\n    \"github.com/redwood-inference/autoscaler/pull/1880\"\n  ],\n  \"dashboards\": [\n    \"console.redwood.internal/d/allocations/reserved-pool-headroom?org=infra\",\n    \"console.redwood.internal/d/alerts/autoscaler-scale-failures?org=infra\"\n  ],\n  \"release\": \"runtime-1.24\",\n  \"security_review_required\": \"false\",\n  \"next_steps\": [\n    \"1) Merge allocator/controller smoothing alignment into stable branch and monitor for regression for 7 days.\",\n    \"2) Implement explicit source-of-truth for burst-credit accounting and add cross-checking telemetry between controller and allocator.\",\n    \"3) Add unit and property tests that simulate sub-2m burst patterns and assert no allocation rejections.\",\n    \"4) Postmortem with NimbusPay and update runbook to include this class of desync.\"\n  ],\n  \"decision_log\": [\n    \"2025-11-05: Decided to prioritize correctness of smoothing math over micro-optimizations that shave latency;       "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Predictive scaling window desync causes reserved-pool shortfalls and customer 5xxs\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-777345-predictive-scale-window-desync-customer-facing.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: engineering\nProject: Dedicated Capacity Stability\nTeam: engineering\n\n# Predictive scaling window desync causes reserved-pool shortfalls and customer 5xxs\n\nKey: ENG-777345\n\nTeam: engineering\n\nTitle: Predictive scaling window desync causes reserved-pool shortfalls and customer 5xxs\n\nStatus: In Progress\n\nPriority: P0\n\nCreated At: 2025-11-04\n\nUpdated At: 2025-11-12\n\nCreator: Ava Thompson\n\nAssignee: Marcus Li\n\nProject: Dedicated Capacity Stability\n\nCycle: 2025-W44\n\nEstimate: 8\n\nDue Date: 2025-11-18\n\n## Labels\n\n- dedicated\n  - autoscaler\n  - reserved-pool\n  - customer-escalation\n  - high-priority\n\nDescription: Summary: During coordinated morning traffic spikes we observed repeated reserved-pool shortfalls for several enterprise tenants (notably NimbusPay and ArbourRetail) that triggered customer-facing 5xx errors and increased latency. Investigation indicates a desynchronization between the predictive autoscaler windowing logic (controller) and the allocator's traffic smoothing/decay function, which resulted in under-provisioned reserved pools for short, high-amplitude bursts. This ticket tracks the bugfix, mitigations, communications, and follow-up hardening work.\n\n## Reproduction Steps\n\n- 1) Use a dedicated tenant with reserved pool enabled and burst credits configured.\n  - 2) Replay a synthetic traffic pattern: 3x baseline QPS for 90s, 1.2x for 10s, then drop to baseline. Repeat on 3-minute cadence.\n  - 3) Observe autoscaler telemetry: controller predicts required headroom but allocator's decay reduces effective headroom quickly; pool size fails to increase fast enough leading to allocation rejections and 5xx gateway errors.\n  - 4) Reproduce across two regions to validate cross-region policy interactions.\n\nCustomer Impact: high",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Predictive scaling window desync causes reserved-pool shortfalls and customer 5xxs\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-777345-predictive-scale-window-desync-customer-facing.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: engineering\nProject: Dedicated Capacity Stability\nTeam: engineering\n\n3) Observe autoscaler telemetry: controller predicts required headroom but allocator's decay reduces effective headroom quickly; pool size fails to increase fast enough leading to allocation rejections and 5xx gateway errors.\n  - 4) Reproduce across two regions to validate cross-region policy interactions.\n\nCustomer Impact: high\n\nImpact Summary: Multiple enterprise customers experienced degraded availability during morning peak windows for ~2 hours across two regions. Error rates spiked to 6-8% for affected routes and some customers reported production incidents. Business impact includes SLA breaches for higher-tier customers and an open escalation with NimbusPay SRE team.\n\nRoot Cause Summary: The predictive autoscaler (controller) and pool allocator use different smoothing/decay implementations and window alignment. Controller forecasts over a 60s lookahead using exponential smoothing with alpha=0.25 anchored on wall-clock buckets; allocator applies a separate decay factor and a 90s effective smoothing that trims recently observed surge signal earlier than the controller expected. During short, high-amplitude bursts the allocator's aggressive decay caused available headroom to be lower than the controller's planned allocation, leading to delayed or insufficient scale-ups. Edge condition: burst-credit accounting also misaligned by one evaluation tick, allowing bursts to exceed intended limits for a few seconds which downstreamed into allocation churn.\n\nMitigation: Short-term: rolled out a cluster-level feature flag disabling allocator aggressive decay for affected regions and applied a conservative safety buffer (+15% headroom) to predictive allocations for enterprise-tier tenants. Communications: notified impacted customers with NRT incident updates and offered 1:1 postmortem. Medium-term: align smoothing windows and source-of-truth for burst-credit consumption between controller and allocator and add a fast-path preemptive scale-up for >2x baseline sustained >30s.\n\n## Timeline",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Predictive scaling window desync causes reserved-pool shortfalls and customer 5xxs\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-777345-predictive-scale-window-desync-customer-facing.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: engineering\nProject: Dedicated Capacity Stability\nTeam: engineering\n\ntenants. Communications: notified impacted customers with NRT incident updates and offered 1:1 postmortem. Medium-term: align smoothing windows and source-of-truth for burst-credit consumption between controller and allocator and add a fast-path preemptive scale-up for >2x baseline sustained >30s.\n\n## Timeline\n\n- 2025-11-04 06:42 UTC: Pager triggered - spikes observed in us-west-2 for reserved pools. NimbusPay SRE reached out via support channel.\n  - 2025-11-04 07:10 UTC: Initial mitigation - enabled safety buffer via runtime config for affected tenants; immediate error rate reduced but not fully resolved.\n  - 2025-11-04 09:30 UTC: Root-cause hypothesis formed: smoothing/window mismatch between controller and allocator.\n  - 2025-11-05 13:00 UTC: Hotfix PR submitted that aligns decay math to controller's exponential smoothing and adds a one-evaluation tick headroom reserve.\n  - 2025-11-06 02:00 UTC: Hotfix deployed to canary clusters in us-west-2 and eu-west-1; observed 90% reduction in allocation rejections.\n  - 2025-11-08 21:15 UTC: Stakeholder review: PM and Reliability approved rollout to remaining regions with gradual ramp.\n  - 2025-11-12 10:00 UTC: Rollout to all regions in progress; monitoring shows stable headroom for 72h window.\n\n## Linked Prs\n\n- github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/6421\n  - github.com/redwood-inference/autoscaler/pull/1880\n\n## Dashboards\n\n- console.redwood.internal/d/allocations/reserved-pool-headroom?org=infra\n  - console.redwood.internal/d/alerts/autoscaler-scale-failures?org=infra\n\nRelease: runtime-1.24\n\nSecurity Review Required: false\n\n## Next Steps",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Predictive scaling window desync causes reserved-pool shortfalls and customer 5xxs\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-777345-predictive-scale-window-desync-customer-facing.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: engineering\nProject: Dedicated Capacity Stability\nTeam: engineering\n\n0\n\n## Dashboards\n\n- console.redwood.internal/d/allocations/reserved-pool-headroom?org=infra\n  - console.redwood.internal/d/alerts/autoscaler-scale-failures?org=infra\n\nRelease: runtime-1.24\n\nSecurity Review Required: false\n\n## Next Steps\n\n- 1) Merge allocator/controller smoothing alignment into stable branch and monitor for regression for 7 days.\n  - 2) Implement explicit source-of-truth for burst-credit accounting and add cross-checking telemetry between controller and allocator.\n  - 3) Add unit and property tests that simulate sub-2m burst patterns and assert no allocation rejections.\n  - 4) Postmortem with NimbusPay and update runbook to include this class of desync.\n\n## Decision Log\n\n- 2025-11-05: Decided to prioritize correctness of smoothing math over micro-optimizations that shave latency; safety buffer accepted as interim tradeoff.\n  - 2025-11-06: Chose staged rollout with canary -> regional -> global to limit blast radius.\n  - 2025-11-10: Agreed to add a focused E2E test harness for burst scenarios in CI.\n\n## Parent Issue\n\n- ENG-673999\n\n## Dependencies\n\n- ENG-55678\n  - ENG-41356\n\nTitle Field Name: title\n\n## Content Field Names\n\n- description\n  - reproduction_steps\n  - impact_summary\n  - root_cause_summary\n  - mitigation\n  - timeline\n  - next_steps\n  - decision_log\n\nDataset Doc Uuid: dsid_fa6744f09ed34014a2cb2c8f2fb979f2",

# Predictive scaling window desync causes reserved-pool shortfalls and customer 5xxs

Key: ENG-777345

Team: engineering

Title: Predictive scaling window desync causes reserved-pool shortfalls and customer 5xxs

Status: In Progress

Priority: P0

Created At: 2025-11-04

Updated At: 2025-11-12

Creator: Ava Thompson

Assignee: Marcus Li

Project: Dedicated Capacity Stability

Cycle: 2025-W44

Estimate: 8

Due Date: 2025-11-18

## Labels

- dedicated
  - autoscaler
  - reserved-pool
  - customer-escalation
  - high-priority

Description: Summary: During coordinated morning traffic spikes we observed repeated reserved-pool shortfalls for several enterprise tenants (notably NimbusPay and ArbourRetail) that triggered customer-facing 5xx errors and increased latency. Investigation indicates a desynchronization between the predictive autoscaler windowing logic (controller) and the allocator's traffic smoothing/decay function, which resulted in under-provisioned reserved pools for short, high-amplitude bursts. This ticket tracks the bugfix, mitigations, communications, and follow-up hardening work.

## Reproduction Steps

- 1) Use a dedicated tenant with reserved pool enabled and burst credits configured.
  - 2) Replay a synthetic traffic pattern: 3x baseline QPS for 90s, 1.2x for 10s, then drop to baseline. Repeat on 3-minute cadence.
  - 3) Observe autoscaler telemetry: controller predicts required headroom but allocator's decay reduces effective headroom quickly; pool size fails to increase fast enough leading to allocation rejections and 5xx gateway errors.
  - 4) Reproduce across two regions to validate cross-region policy interactions.

Customer Impact: high

3) Observe autoscaler telemetry: controller predicts required headroom but allocator's decay reduces effective headroom quickly; pool size fails to increase fast enough leading to allocation rejections and 5xx gateway errors.
  - 4) Reproduce across two regions to validate cross-region policy interactions.

Customer Impact: high

Impact Summary: Multiple enterprise customers experienced degraded availability during morning peak windows for ~2 hours across two regions. Error rates spiked to 6-8% for affected routes and some customers reported production incidents. Business impact includes SLA breaches for higher-tier customers and an open escalation with NimbusPay SRE team.

Root Cause Summary: The predictive autoscaler (controller) and pool allocator use different smoothing/decay implementations and window alignment. Controller forecasts over a 60s lookahead using exponential smoothing with alpha=0.25 anchored on wall-clock buckets; allocator applies a separate decay factor and a 90s effective smoothing that trims recently observed surge signal earlier than the controller expected. During short, high-amplitude bursts the allocator's aggressive decay caused available headroom to be lower than the controller's planned allocation, leading to delayed or insufficient scale-ups. Edge condition: burst-credit accounting also misaligned by one evaluation tick, allowing bursts to exceed intended limits for a few seconds which downstreamed into allocation churn.

Mitigation: Short-term: rolled out a cluster-level feature flag disabling allocator aggressive decay for affected regions and applied a conservative safety buffer (+15% headroom) to predictive allocations for enterprise-tier tenants. Communications: notified impacted customers with NRT incident updates and offered 1:1 postmortem. Medium-term: align smoothing windows and source-of-truth for burst-credit consumption between controller and allocator and add a fast-path preemptive scale-up for >2x baseline sustained >30s.

## Timeline

{
  "document": {
    "id": "dsid_747bd6fada5d46c7a5021901a98769ba",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-autoscaling-bounds-precedence-and-safety-invariants.json",
    "title": "ADR-047: Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds — Precedence and Safety Invariants",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"ADR-047: Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds \\u2014 Precedence and Safety Invariants\",\n  \"space\": \"architecture-and-standards\",\n  \"author\": \"Rafael Mendes\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2025-06-24\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2025-08-06\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Vanessa Ortiz\",\n    \"Keiko Yamamoto\",\n    \"Ethan Park\",\n    \"Lauren Bishop\",\n    \"Allison Grant\",\n    \"Miles Thornton\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"adr\",\n    \"dedicated\",\n    \"autoscaling\",\n    \"capacity\",\n    \"safety-invariants\",\n    \"predictive-scaling\",\n    \"control-plane\"\n  ],\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"sources/confluence/product-docs/design-specs/autoscaling-policy-schema-and-console-ux.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/autoscaler-bounds-and-predictive-signals-architecture.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/capacity-policy-service.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/observability-standards/metric-naming-for-scaling-and-capacity.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/dedicated-autoscaling-slo-and-alerting-updates.json\"\n  ],\n  \"body\": \"## Summary\\nThis ADR defines the **authoritative semantics** for customer-configurable autoscaling bounds (min/max) for **Redwood Dedicated** deployments, including:\\n- Precedence between customer bounds and platform defaults\\n- Conflict resolution between **predictive** and **reactive** scaling signals\\n- Safety invariants for scale-down (and scale-up) behavior\\n- Deterministic evaluation requirements for auditability\\n\\nThe goal is to provide enterprise-grade, contract-aligned guardrails that are **hard enforced**, **observable**, and **operationally safe**.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Status\\n**Accepted** (implemented behind feature flags; required for GA).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Context\\nRedwood Dedicated historically relies on platform-driven autoscaling (reactive metrics + operator overrides). Enterprise customers require:\\n- A **hard maximum** to prevent unexpected spend and enforce contractual ceilings.\\n- A **hard minimum** to ensure baseline capacity and avoid cold-start latency.\\n- Optional **predictive scaling** to pre-warm capacity ahead of known ramps, without sacrificing reliability.\\n\\nThis introduces several ambiguous cases that must be explicitly defined:\\n- What happens when the platform \\u201cwants\\u201d to scale outside customer bounds?\\n- What if predictive suggests scaling down but reactive signals indicate saturation?\\n- What if the fleet cannot provision the customer minimum due to a region capacity shortage?\\n- How do we avoid oscillation and unsafe scale-to-zero outcomes?\\n\\nThis ADR clarifies these semantics and the precedence ordering to enable consistent implementation in the autoscaler loop, the control plane policy evaluator, Console UX, and on-call procedures.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Decision\\n### D1. Customer bounds are **hard constraints** on desired capacity\\nFor a Dedicated deployment with customer bounds:\\n- Autoscaler MUST NOT set desired replicas below `min_replicas`.\\n- Autoscaler MUST NOT set desired replicas above `max_replicas`.\\n- Bounds apply regardless of the source of desired capacity (reactive, predictive, operator, or platform defaults).\\n\\n**Canonical clamp:**\\n`bounded_desired = clamp(requested_desired, min_replicas, max_replicas)`\\n\\nWhere:\\n- `requested_desired` is the desired replica count computed prior to bounds enforcement.\\n- `bounded_desired` is the desired replica count after applying hard bounds.\\n\\n### D2. Precedence order for computing requested_desired\\nThe autoscaler computes `requested_desired` using the following precedence and arbitration rules:\\n\\n1) **Hard safety overrides (scale-up only)**\\n   - If reactive overload signals exceed critical thresholds (e.g., sustained queue growth / saturation), autoscaler may request an *immediate* scale-up (subject to `max_replicas`).\\n\\n2) **Predictive desired (if enabled and valid)**\\n   - If predictive mode is enabled and the forecast is \\u201cvalid\\u201d (fresh, confidence >= minimum, model coverage OK), compute a predictive desired target.\\n\\n3) **Reactive desired (always available)**\\n   - Compute reactive desired from observed metrics (queue depth, utilization/saturation, latency signals) using the standard control loop.\\n\\n4) **Arbitration between predictive and reactive**\\n   - Requested desired is the **max()** of predictive and reactive desired for scale-up decisions.\\n   - For scale-down decisions, requested desired is the **min()** of predictive and reactive desired, *subject to scale-down safety rules in D4*.\\n\\nRationale: predictive is intended to avoid under-provisioning during ramps, but reactive must still prevent overload if predictions are wrong. For scale-down, we are conservative to prevent churn and under-provisioning.\\n\\n### D3. Platform defaults do not override explicit customer bounds\\nPlatform defaults (e.g., recommended min, recommended max, default cooldowns) are used only when the customer has not set an explicit value.\\n\\nEffective policy fields:\\n- If customer specifies `min_replicas`, it replaces the platform default min.\\n- If customer specifies `max_replicas`, it replaces the platform default max.\\n- If a field is unset, platform default applies.\\n\\nConsole MUST display both:\\n- Customer-configured values (explicit)\\n- Platform recommended range (informational only)\\n\\n### D4. Scale-down safety invariants\\nScale-down MUST be more conservative than scale-up.\\n\\nRequired invariants:\\n- Never scale down below `min_replicas`.\\n- Never scale down if the deployment is in an overload condition (reactive critical signals active).\\n- Never scale down more than `max_scale_down_step` per control interval.\\n- Enforce cooldowns and dampening (see D5).\\n\\nAdditionally:\\n- If predictive returns null/unknown, it MUST NOT contribute to scale-down (treat as \\u201cno opinion\\u201d).\\n- If predictive is stale or confidence is below threshold, predictive MUST be ignored (fallback to reactive).\\n\\n### D5. Anti-oscillation guardrails are mandatory\\nTo prevent oscillation caused by noisy signals or forecast error:\\n- Enforce separate cooldown windows for scale-up and scale-down (e.g., 60s up, 300s down; exact values may vary by tier but MUST be non-zero).\\n- Apply smoothing/dampening to reactive signals (e.g., EWMA) and require sustained conditions for scale-down.\\n- Require minimum step sizing (avoid 1-replica flapping) unless in critical overload.\\n\\n### D6. Shortage behavior when minimum cannot be met\\nIf the fleet cannot provision `min_replicas` due to region capacity shortage:\\n- Autoscaler MUST continue to *request* at least `min_replicas`.\\n- System MUST surface a degraded state: `min_unmet` (with reason code: `REGION_SHORTAGE`, `QUOTA`, `PLACEMENT_FAILURE`, etc.).\\n- SRE alerts MUST trigger based on `min_unmet` duration and customer impact.\\n- Smart routing MAY use bounded-state signals for graceful degradation (e.g., fallback to compatible model/region per customer policy), but MUST NOT violate customer bounds within the Dedicated deployment.\\n\\n### D7. Deterministic evaluation + auditability is required\\nFor every autoscaler decision cycle (or at minimum every effective change), the system MUST record:\\n- `requested_desired`\\n- `bounded_desired`\\n- Active bounds (`min_replicas`, `max_replicas`)\\n- Signal inputs and reason codes (predictive_valid, reactive_overload, cooldown_blocked, min_unmet, max_hit)\\n- Whether the decision resulted in a scale event\\n\\nThese records must be queryable for enterprise support and compliance review.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Definitions\\n- **Replicas:** number of serving instances backing a Dedicated deployment (GPU-backed workers).\\n- **Requested desired:** desired replica count before bounds enforcement.\\n- **Bounded desired:** desired replica count after hard clamp to [min, max].\\n- **Reactive signals:** real-time metrics (queue depth, saturation/utilization, latency, error rate) feeding the autoscaler control loop.\\n- **Predictive signals:** forecasted demand (time-of-day patterns, scheduled events, historical trends) producing a target capacity ahead of observed load.\\n- **Overload condition:** sustained indicators that the system is under-provisioned (e.g., queue growth + saturation + latency regression).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Precedence and conflict resolution (normative)\\n### Capacity computation sequence\\n1. Load effective scaling policy (post-validation).\\n2. Compute `reactive_desired`.\\n3. If predictive enabled and forecast valid, compute `predictive_desired`.\\n4. Compute `requested_desired`:\\n   - If overload critical: `requested_desired = max(reactive_desired, predictive_desired_if_any)` with overload step-up allowed.\\n   - Else:\\n     - For upward moves: `requested_desired = max(reactive_desired, predictive_desired_if_any)`\\n     - For downward moves: `requested_desired = min(reactive_desired, predictive_desired_if_any)` but blocked by scale-down safety rules.\\n5. Apply clamp to produce `bounded_desired`.\\n6. Apply cooldowns / dampening gates.\\n7. Emit decision record + metrics.\\n\\n### Bounds enforcement is always last\\nBounds are applied after we compute requested desired, but before we actuate scaling.\\n\\nThis ensures:\\n- Audit logs can show when the system *wanted* to scale beyond a bound.\\n- Metrics can track bound-hit rates.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Safety invariants (must-hold)\\nThe following are invariants the autoscaler MUST enforce:\\n1) **Never exceed max:** `bounded_desired <= max_replicas` at all times.\\n2) **Never drop below min:** `bounded_desired >= min_replicas` at all times.\\n3) **No scale-to-zero when bounds enabled:** if `min_replicas >= 1`, scale-to-zero is forbidden.\\n4) **No unsafe scale-down during overload:** scale-down is blocked when reactive overload signals are active.\\n5) **Deterministic decisions:** given the same policy + inputs at time T, evaluator yields the same requested/bounded desired and reason codes.\\n6) **Fallback correctness:** if predictive is unavailable/stale/invalid, behavior equals reactive mode (still respecting bounds).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Observability requirements (decision-linked)\\nThe following telemetry MUST be emitted:\\n- Gauge: desired replicas (requested vs bounded)\\n- Counter: bound hit events (`max_hit`, `min_hit`)\\n- Gauge: forecast freshness and confidence\\n- Gauge/counter: prediction error (forecast vs realized)\\n- Counter: decision reason codes (cooldown_blocked, overload_override, predictive_invalid, etc.)\\n- Gauge: `min_unmet` and associated reason\\n\\nMetric naming and label limits MUST follow the observability standard referenced in related pages (avoid unbounded cardinality).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Alternatives considered\\n### A1. Soft bounds (warnings only)\\nRejected. Customer requirement is contractual guardrails; soft bounds do not meet budget-capping and baseline guarantees.\\n\\n### A2. Predictive overrides reactive (prediction wins)\\nRejected. Reactive metrics are required to prevent overload when predictions are wrong; predictive must not force scale-down into saturation.\\n\\n### A3. Clamp first, then compute predictive/reactive\\nRejected. Clamping early hides the platform\\u2019s \\u201crequested desired\\u201d intent and reduces auditability (cannot reason about why latency regressed while max-bound was hit).\\n\\n### A4. Scale-up uses max(predictive, reactive), scale-down uses reactive only\\nNot selected as the default. We allow predictive input into scale-down only when it is valid and scale-down safety gates pass; however, the net effect is still conservative due to cooldown and overload blocks.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Consequences\\n### Positive\\n- Customers get deterministic, enforceable behavior aligned with contracts.\\n- Support and SRE can quickly diagnose \\u201cwe hit max\\u201d vs \\u201cprediction stale\\u201d vs \\u201cregion shortage.\\u201d\\n- Predictive scaling can improve p95 latency during known ramps while maintaining safety.\\n\\n### Tradeoffs / risks\\n- Customers can misconfigure bounds (e.g., min too high), increasing shortage risk.\\n- Hard max may cap performance during unexpected spikes (intentional by contract); requires clear UX and CS guidance.\\n- Conservative scale-down may increase cost slightly vs aggressive reactive downscaling.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Rollout and compatibility notes\\n- Existing Dedicated deployments retain current behavior until the feature flag is enabled.\\n- On enablement, defaults must preserve behavior unless customer explicitly sets bounds.\\n- During pilot, require SRE readiness review and alert tuning before expanding to additional accounts.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Open questions (tracked outside ADR)\\n- Exact default cooldowns and step sizes per model family / GPU type (performance tuning doc).\\n- Whether max should be expressed in replicas, GPUs, or both (schema evolution).\\n- Smart routing policy interactions during `min_unmet` and `max_hit` states (routing ADR).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Appendix: Reason codes (initial set)\\nAutoscaler decision records SHOULD include one or more of:\\n- `PREDICTIVE_VALID`\\n- `PREDICTIVE_INVALID_STALE`\\n- `PREDICTIVE_INVALID_LOW_CONFIDENCE`\\n- `REACTIVE_OVERLOAD_CRITICAL`\\n- `SCALE_UP`\\n- `SCALE_DOWN`\\n- `COOLDOWN_BLOCKED_UP`\\n- `COOLDOWN_BLOCKED_DOWN`\\n- `MAX_BOUND_HIT`\\n- `MIN_BOUND_HIT`\\n- `MIN_UNMET_REGION_SHORTAGE`\\n- `MIN_UNMET_PLACEMENT_FAILURE`\\n\\n(Reason code list is extensible but must remain stable enough for dashboards and runbooks.)\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_747bd6fada5d46c7a5021901a98769ba\"\n}",

sources/confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/dedicated-autoscaling-slo-and-alerting-updates.json\n\nBody: ## Summary\nThis ADR defines the **authoritative semantics** for customer-configurable autoscaling bounds (min/max) for **Redwood Dedicated** deployments, including:\n- Precedence between customer bounds and platform defaults\n- Conflict resolution between **predictive** and **reactive** scaling signals\n- Safety invariants for scale-down (and scale-up) behavior\n- Deterministic evaluation requirements for auditability\n\nThe goal is to provide enterprise-grade, contract-aligned guardrails that are **hard enforced**, **observable**, and **operationally safe**.\n\n---\n\n## Status\n**Accepted** (implemented behind feature flags; required for GA).\n\n---",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: ADR-047: Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds — Precedence and Safety Invariants\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-autoscaling-bounds-precedence-and-safety-invariants.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: architecture-and-standards\n\nand scale-up) behavior\n- Deterministic evaluation requirements for auditability\n\nThe goal is to provide enterprise-grade, contract-aligned guardrails that are **hard enforced**, **observable**, and **operationally safe**.\n\n---\n\n## Status\n**Accepted** (implemented behind feature flags; required for GA).\n\n---\n\n## Context\nRedwood Dedicated historically relies on platform-driven autoscaling (reactive metrics + operator overrides). Enterprise customers require:\n- A **hard maximum** to prevent unexpected spend and enforce contractual ceilings.\n- A **hard minimum** to ensure baseline capacity and avoid cold-start latency.\n- Optional **predictive scaling** to pre-warm capacity ahead of known ramps, without sacrificing reliability.\n\nThis introduces several ambiguous cases that must be explicitly defined:\n- What happens when the platform “wants” to scale outside customer bounds?\n- What if predictive suggests scaling down but reactive signals indicate saturation?\n- What if the fleet cannot provision the customer minimum due to a region capacity shortage?\n- How do we avoid oscillation and unsafe scale-to-zero outcomes?\n\nThis ADR clarifies these semantics and the precedence ordering to enable consistent implementation in the autoscaler loop, the control plane policy evaluator, Console UX, and on-call procedures.\n\n---\n\n## Decision\n### D1. Customer bounds are **hard constraints** on desired capacity\nFor a Dedicated deployment with customer bounds:\n- Autoscaler MUST NOT set desired replicas below `min_replicas`.\n- Autoscaler MUST NOT set desired replicas above `max_replicas`.\n- Bounds apply regardless of the source of desired capacity (reactive, predictive, operator, or platform defaults).\n\n**Canonical clamp:**\n`bounded_desired = clamp(requested_desired, min_replicas, max_replicas)`\n\nWhere:\n- `requested_desired` is the desired replica count computed prior to bounds enforcement.\n- `bounded_desired` is the desired replica count after applying hard bounds.\n\n### D2.       "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: ADR-047: Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds — Precedence and Safety Invariants\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-autoscaling-bounds-precedence-and-safety-invariants.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: architecture-and-standards\n\n`requested_desired` is the desired replica count computed prior to bounds enforcement.\n- `bounded_desired` is the desired replica count after applying hard bounds.\n\n### D2. Precedence order for computing requested_desired\nThe autoscaler computes `requested_desired` using the following precedence and arbitration rules:\n\n1) **Hard safety overrides (scale-up only)**\n   - If reactive overload signals exceed critical thresholds (e.g., sustained queue growth / saturation), autoscaler may request an *immediate* scale-up (subject to `max_replicas`).\n\n2) **Predictive desired (if enabled and valid)**\n   - If predictive mode is enabled and the forecast is “valid” (fresh, confidence >= minimum, model coverage OK), compute a predictive desired target.\n\n3) **Reactive desired (always available)**\n   - Compute reactive desired from observed metrics (queue depth, utilization/saturation, latency signals) using the standard control loop.\n\n4) **Arbitration between predictive and reactive**\n   - Requested desired is the **max()** of predictive and reactive desired for scale-up decisions.\n   - For scale-down decisions, requested desired is the **min()** of predictive and reactive desired, *subject to scale-down safety rules in D4*.\n\nRationale: predictive is intended to avoid under-provisioning during ramps, but reactive must still prevent overload if predictions are wrong. For scale-down, we are conservative to prevent churn and under-provisioning.\n\n### D3. Platform defaults do not override explicit customer bounds\nPlatform defaults (e.g., recommended min, recommended max, default cooldowns) are used only when the customer has not set an explicit value.\n\nEffective policy fields:\n- If customer specifies `min_replicas`, it replaces the platform default min.\n- If customer specifies `max_replicas`, it replaces the platform default max.\n- If a field is unset, platform default applies.\n\nConsole MUST display both:\n- Customer-configured values (explicit)\n- Platform recommended range (informational only)",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: ADR-047: Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds — Precedence and Safety Invariants\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-autoscaling-bounds-precedence-and-safety-invariants.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: architecture-and-standards\n\ncustomer specifies `min_replicas`, it replaces the platform default min.\n- If customer specifies `max_replicas`, it replaces the platform default max.\n- If a field is unset, platform default applies.\n\nConsole MUST display both:\n- Customer-configured values (explicit)\n- Platform recommended range (informational only)\n\n### D4. Scale-down safety invariants\nScale-down MUST be more conservative than scale-up.\n\nRequired invariants:\n- Never scale down below `min_replicas`.\n- Never scale down if the deployment is in an overload condition (reactive critical signals active).\n- Never scale down more than `max_scale_down_step` per control interval.\n- Enforce cooldowns and dampening (see D5).\n\nAdditionally:\n- If predictive returns null/unknown, it MUST NOT contribute to scale-down (treat as “no opinion”).\n- If predictive is stale or confidence is below threshold, predictive MUST be ignored (fallback to reactive).\n\n### D5. Anti-oscillation guardrails are mandatory\nTo prevent oscillation caused by noisy signals or forecast error:\n- Enforce separate cooldown windows for scale-up and scale-down (e.g., 60s up, 300s down; exact values may vary by tier but MUST be non-zero).\n- Apply smoothing/dampening to reactive signals (e.g., EWMA) and require sustained conditions for scale-down.\n- Require minimum step sizing (avoid 1-replica flapping) unless in critical overload.",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: ADR-047: Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds — Precedence and Safety Invariants\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-autoscaling-bounds-precedence-and-safety-invariants.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: architecture-and-standards\n\ns up, 300s down; exact values may vary by tier but MUST be non-zero).\n- Apply smoothing/dampening to reactive signals (e.g., EWMA) and require sustained conditions for scale-down.\n- Require minimum step sizing (avoid 1-replica flapping) unless in critical overload.\n\n### D6. Shortage behavior when minimum cannot be met\nIf the fleet cannot provision `min_replicas` due to region capacity shortage:\n- Autoscaler MUST continue to *request* at least `min_replicas`.\n- System MUST surface a degraded state: `min_unmet` (with reason code: `REGION_SHORTAGE`, `QUOTA`, `PLACEMENT_FAILURE`, etc.).\n- SRE alerts MUST trigger based on `min_unmet` duration and customer impact.\n- Smart routing MAY use bounded-state signals for graceful degradation (e.g., fallback to compatible model/region per customer policy), but MUST NOT violate customer bounds within the Dedicated deployment.\n\n### D7. Deterministic evaluation + auditability is required\nFor every autoscaler decision cycle (or at minimum every effective change), the system MUST record:\n- `requested_desired`\n- `bounded_desired`\n- Active bounds (`min_replicas`, `max_replicas`)\n- Signal inputs and reason codes (predictive_valid, reactive_overload, cooldown_blocked, min_unmet, max_hit)\n- Whether the decision resulted in a scale event\n\nThese records must be queryable for enterprise support and compliance review.\n\n---",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: ADR-047: Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds — Precedence and Safety Invariants\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-autoscaling-bounds-precedence-and-safety-invariants.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: architecture-and-standards\n\n`\n- Active bounds (`min_replicas`, `max_replicas`)\n- Signal inputs and reason codes (predictive_valid, reactive_overload, cooldown_blocked, min_unmet, max_hit)\n- Whether the decision resulted in a scale event\n\nThese records must be queryable for enterprise support and compliance review.\n\n---\n\n## Definitions\n- **Replicas:** number of serving instances backing a Dedicated deployment (GPU-backed workers).\n- **Requested desired:** desired replica count before bounds enforcement.\n- **Bounded desired:** desired replica count after hard clamp to [min, max].\n- **Reactive signals:** real-time metrics (queue depth, saturation/utilization, latency, error rate) feeding the autoscaler control loop.\n- **Predictive signals:** forecasted demand (time-of-day patterns, scheduled events, historical trends) producing a target capacity ahead of observed load.\n- **Overload condition:** sustained indicators that the system is under-provisioned (e.g., queue growth + saturation + latency regression).\n\n---\n\n## Precedence and conflict resolution (normative)\n### Capacity computation sequence\n1. Load effective scaling policy (post-validation).\n2. Compute `reactive_desired`.\n3. If predictive enabled and forecast valid, compute `predictive_desired`.\n4. Compute `requested_desired`:\n   - If overload critical: `requested_desired = max(reactive_desired, predictive_desired_if_any)` with overload step-up allowed.\n   - Else:\n     - For upward moves: `requested_desired = max(reactive_desired, predictive_desired_if_any)`\n     - For downward moves: `requested_desired = min(reactive_desired, predictive_desired_if_any)` but blocked by scale-down safety rules.\n5. Apply clamp to produce `bounded_desired`.\n6. Apply cooldowns / dampening gates.\n7. Emit decision record + metrics.\n\n### Bounds enforcement is always last\nBounds are applied after we compute requested desired, but before we actuate scaling.",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: ADR-047: Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds — Precedence and Safety Invariants\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-autoscaling-bounds-precedence-and-safety-invariants.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: architecture-and-standards\n\n_if_any)` but blocked by scale-down safety rules.\n5. Apply clamp to produce `bounded_desired`.\n6. Apply cooldowns / dampening gates.\n7. Emit decision record + metrics.\n\n### Bounds enforcement is always last\nBounds are applied after we compute requested desired, but before we actuate scaling.\n\nThis ensures:\n- Audit logs can show when the system *wanted* to scale beyond a bound.\n- Metrics can track bound-hit rates.\n\n---\n\n## Safety invariants (must-hold)\nThe following are invariants the autoscaler MUST enforce:\n1) **Never exceed max:** `bounded_desired <= max_replicas` at all times.\n2) **Never drop below min:** `bounded_desired >= min_replicas` at all times.\n3) **No scale-to-zero when bounds enabled:** if `min_replicas >= 1`, scale-to-zero is forbidden.\n4) **No unsafe scale-down during overload:** scale-down is blocked when reactive overload signals are active.\n5) **Deterministic decisions:** given the same policy + inputs at time T, evaluator yields the same requested/bounded desired and reason codes.\n6) **Fallback correctness:** if predictive is unavailable/stale/invalid, behavior equals reactive mode (still respecting bounds).\n\n---\n\n## Observability requirements (decision-linked)\nThe following telemetry MUST be emitted:\n- Gauge: desired replicas (requested vs bounded)\n- Counter: bound hit events (`max_hit`, `min_hit`)\n- Gauge: forecast freshness and confidence\n- Gauge/counter: prediction error (forecast vs realized)\n- Counter: decision reason codes (cooldown_blocked, overload_override, predictive_invalid, etc.)\n- Gauge: `min_unmet` and associated reason\n\nMetric naming and label limits MUST follow the observability standard referenced in related pages (avoid unbounded cardinality).\n\n---\n\n## Alternatives considered\n### A1. Soft bounds (warnings only)\nRejected. Customer requirement is contractual guardrails; soft bounds do not meet budget-capping and baseline guarantees.",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: ADR-047: Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds — Precedence and Safety Invariants\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-autoscaling-bounds-precedence-and-safety-invariants.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: architecture-and-standards\n\nassociated reason\n\nMetric naming and label limits MUST follow the observability standard referenced in related pages (avoid unbounded cardinality).\n\n---\n\n## Alternatives considered\n### A1. Soft bounds (warnings only)\nRejected. Customer requirement is contractual guardrails; soft bounds do not meet budget-capping and baseline guarantees.\n\n### A2. Predictive overrides reactive (prediction wins)\nRejected. Reactive metrics are required to prevent overload when predictions are wrong; predictive must not force scale-down into saturation.\n\n### A3. Clamp first, then compute predictive/reactive\nRejected. Clamping early hides the platform’s “requested desired” intent and reduces auditability (cannot reason about why latency regressed while max-bound was hit).\n\n### A4. Scale-up uses max(predictive, reactive), scale-down uses reactive only\nNot selected as the default. We allow predictive input into scale-down only when it is valid and scale-down safety gates pass; however, the net effect is still conservative due to cooldown and overload blocks.\n\n---\n\n## Consequences\n### Positive\n- Customers get deterministic, enforceable behavior aligned with contracts.\n- Support and SRE can quickly diagnose “we hit max” vs “prediction stale” vs “region shortage.”\n- Predictive scaling can improve p95 latency during known ramps while maintaining safety.\n\n### Tradeoffs / risks\n- Customers can misconfigure bounds (e.g., min too high), increasing shortage risk.\n- Hard max may cap performance during unexpected spikes (intentional by contract); requires clear UX and CS guidance.\n- Conservative scale-down may increase cost slightly vs aggressive reactive downscaling.\n\n---\n\n## Rollout and compatibility notes\n- Existing Dedicated deployments retain current behavior until the feature flag is enabled.\n- On enablement, defaults must preserve behavior unless customer explicitly sets bounds.\n- During pilot, require SRE readiness review and alert tuning before expanding to additional accounts.\n\n---",

      "ordinal": 8,
      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: ADR-047: Dedicated Autoscaling Bounds — Precedence and Safety Invariants\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-autoscaling-bounds-precedence-and-safety-invariants.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: architecture-and-standards\n\naggressive reactive downscaling.\n\n---\n\n## Rollout and compatibility notes\n- Existing Dedicated deployments retain current behavior until the feature flag is enabled.\n- On enablement, defaults must preserve behavior unless customer explicitly sets bounds.\n- During pilot, require SRE readiness review and alert tuning before expanding to additional accounts.\n\n---\n\n## Open questions (tracked outside ADR)\n- Exact default cooldowns and step sizes per model family / GPU type (performance tuning doc).\n- Whether max should be expressed in replicas, GPUs, or both (schema evolution).\n- Smart routing policy interactions during `min_unmet` and `max_hit` states (routing ADR).\n\n---\n\n## Appendix: Reason codes (initial set)\nAutoscaler decision records SHOULD include one or more of:\n- `PREDICTIVE_VALID`\n- `PREDICTIVE_INVALID_STALE`\n- `PREDICTIVE_INVALID_LOW_CONFIDENCE`\n- `REACTIVE_OVERLOAD_CRITICAL`\n- `SCALE_UP`\n- `SCALE_DOWN`\n- `COOLDOWN_BLOCKED_UP`\n- `COOLDOWN_BLOCKED_DOWN`\n- `MAX_BOUND_HIT`\n- `MIN_BOUND_HIT`\n- `MIN_UNMET_REGION_SHORTAGE`\n- `MIN_UNMET_PLACEMENT_FAILURE`\n\n(Reason code list is extensible but must remain stable enough for dashboards and runbooks.)\n\nTitle Field Name: title\n\n## Content Field Names\n\n- body\n\nDataset Doc Uuid: dsid_747bd6fada5d46c7a5021901a98769ba",

{

  "space": "architecture-and-standards",
  "author": "Rafael Mendes",
  "owner_team": "engineering",
  "status": "published",

  "created_at": "2025-06-24",
  "last_updated": "2025-08-06",

    "sources/confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/capacity-policy-service.json",

  "body": "## Summary
This ADR defines the **authoritative semantics** for customer-configurable autoscaling bounds (min/max) for **Redwood Dedicated** deployments, including:
- Precedence between customer bounds and platform defaults
- Conflict resolution between **predictive** and **reactive** scaling signals
- Safety invariants for scale-down (and scale-up) behavior
- Deterministic evaluation requirements for auditability

The goal is to provide enterprise-grade, contract-aligned guardrails that are **hard enforced**, **observable**, and **operationally safe**.

---

## Status
**Accepted** (implemented behind feature flags; required for GA).

---

## Context
Redwood Dedicated historically relies on platform-driven autoscaling (reactive metrics + operator overrides). Enterprise customers require:
- A **hard maximum** to prevent unexpected spend and enforce contractual ceilings.
- A **hard minimum** to ensure baseline capacity and avoid cold-start latency.
- Optional **predictive scaling** to pre-warm capacity ahead of known ramps, without sacrificing reliability.

This introduces several ambiguous cases that must be explicitly defined:
- What happens when the platform “wants” to scale outside customer bounds?
- What if predictive suggests scaling down but reactive signals indicate saturation?
- What if the fleet cannot provision the customer minimum due to a region capacity shortage?
- How do we avoid oscillation and unsafe scale-to-zero outcomes?

This ADR clarifies these semantics and the precedence ordering to enable consistent implementation in the autoscaler loop, the control plane policy evaluator, Console UX, and on-call procedures.

---

## Decision
### D1. Customer bounds are **hard constraints** on desired capacity
For a Dedicated deployment with customer bounds:
- Autoscaler MUST NOT set desired replicas below `min_replicas`.
- Autoscaler MUST NOT set desired replicas above `max_replicas`.
- Bounds apply regardless of the source of desired capacity (reactive, predictive, operator, or platform defaults).

**Canonical clamp:**
`bounded_desired = clamp(requested_desired, min_replicas, max_replicas)`

Where:
- `requested_desired` is the desired replica count computed prior to bounds enforcement.
- `bounded_desired` is the desired replica count after applying hard bounds.

### D2. Precedence order for computing requested_desired
The autoscaler computes `requested_desired` using the following precedence and arbitration rules:

1) **Hard safety overrides (scale-up only)**
   - If reactive overload signals exceed critical thresholds (e.g., sustained queue growth / saturation), autoscaler may request an *immediate* scale-up (subject to `max_replicas`).

2) **Predictive desired (if enabled and valid)**
   - If predictive mode is enabled and the forecast is “valid” (fresh, confidence >= minimum, model coverage OK), compute a predictive desired target.

3) **Reactive desired (always available)**
   - Compute reactive desired from observed metrics (queue depth, utilization/saturation, latency signals) using the standard control loop.

4) **Arbitration between predictive and reactive**
   - Requested desired is the **max()** of predictive and reactive desired for scale-up decisions.
   - For scale-down decisions, requested desired is the **min()** of predictive and reactive desired, *subject to scale-down safety rules in D4*.

Rationale: predictive is intended to avoid under-provisioning during ramps, but reactive must still prevent overload if predictions are wrong. For scale-down, we are conservative to prevent churn and under-provisioning.

### D3. Platform defaults do not override explicit customer bounds
Platform defaults (e.g., recommended min, recommended max, default cooldowns) are used only when the customer has not set an explicit value.

Effective policy fields:
- If customer specifies `min_replicas`, it replaces the platform default min.
- If customer specifies `max_replicas`, it replaces the platform default max.
- If a field is unset, platform default applies.

Console MUST display both:
- Customer-configured values (explicit)
- Platform recommended range (informational only)

### D4. Scale-down safety invariants
Scale-down MUST be more conservative than scale-up.

Required invariants:
- Never scale down below `min_replicas`.
- Never scale down if the deployment is in an overload condition (reactive critical signals active).
- Never scale down more than `max_scale_down_step` per control interval.
- Enforce cooldowns and dampening (see D5).

Additionally:
- If predictive returns null/unknown, it MUST NOT contribute to scale-down (treat as “no opinion”).
- If predictive is stale or confidence is below threshold, predictive MUST be ignored (fallback to reactive).

### D5. Anti-oscillation guardrails are mandatory
To prevent oscillation caused by noisy signals or forecast error:
- Enforce separate cooldown windows for scale-up and scale-down (e.g., 60s up, 300s down; exact values may vary by tier but MUST be non-zero).
- Apply smoothing/dampening to reactive signals (e.g., EWMA) and require sustained conditions for scale-down.
- Require minimum step sizing (avoid 1-replica flapping) unless in critical overload.

### D6. Shortage behavior when minimum cannot be met
If the fleet cannot provision `min_replicas` due to region capacity shortage:
- Autoscaler MUST continue to *request* at least `min_replicas`.
- System MUST surface a degraded state: `min_unmet` (with reason code: `REGION_SHORTAGE`, `QUOTA`, `PLACEMENT_FAILURE`, etc.).
- SRE alerts MUST trigger based on `min_unmet` duration and customer impact.
- Smart routing MAY use bounded-state signals for graceful degradation (e.g., fallback to compatible model/region per customer policy), but MUST NOT violate customer bounds within the Dedicated deployment.

### D7. Deterministic evaluation + auditability is required
For every autoscaler decision cycle (or at minimum every effective change), the system MUST record:
- `requested_desired`
- `bounded_desired`
- Active bounds (`min_replicas`, `max_replicas`)
- Signal inputs and reason codes (predictive_valid, reactive_overload, cooldown_blocked, min_unmet, max_hit)
- Whether the decision resulted in a scale event

These records must be queryable for enterprise support and compliance review.

---

## Definitions
- **Replicas:** number of serving instances backing a Dedicated deployment (GPU-backed workers).
- **Requested desired:** desired replica count before bounds enforcement.
- **Bounded desired:** desired replica count after hard clamp to [min, max].
- **Reactive signals:** real-time metrics (queue depth, saturation/utilization, latency, error rate) feeding the autoscaler control loop.
- **Predictive signals:** forecasted demand (time-of-day patterns, scheduled events, historical trends) producing a target capacity ahead of observed load.
- **Overload condition:** sustained indicators that the system is under-provisioned (e.g., queue growth + saturation + latency regression).

---

## Precedence and conflict resolution (normative)
### Capacity computation sequence
1. Load effective scaling policy (post-validation).
2. Compute `reactive_desired`.
3. If predictive enabled and forecast valid, compute `predictive_desired`.
4. Compute `requested_desired`:
   - If overload critical: `requested_desired = max(reactive_desired, predictive_desired_if_any)` with overload step-up allowed.
   - Else:
     - For upward moves: `requested_desired = max(reactive_desired, predictive_desired_if_any)`
     - For downward moves: `requested_desired = min(reactive_desired, predictive_desired_if_any)` but blocked by scale-down safety rules.
5. Apply clamp to produce `bounded_desired`.
6. Apply cooldowns / dampening gates.
7. Emit decision record + metrics.

### Bounds enforcement is always last
Bounds are applied after we compute requested desired, but before we actuate scaling.

This ensures:
- Audit logs can show when the system *wanted* to scale beyond a bound.
- Metrics can track bound-hit rates.

---

## Safety invariants (must-hold)
The following are invariants the autoscaler MUST enforce:
1) **Never exceed max:** `bounded_desired <= max_replicas` at all times.
2) **Never drop below min:** `bounded_desired >= min_replicas` at all times.
3) **No scale-to-zero when bounds enabled:** if `min_replicas >= 1`, scale-to-zero is forbidden.
4) **No unsafe scale-down during overload:** scale-down is blocked when reactive overload signals are active.
5) **Deterministic decisions:** given the same policy + inputs at time T, evaluator yields the same requested/bounded desired and reason codes.
6) **Fallback correctness:** if predictive is unavailable/stale/invalid, behavior equals reactive mode (still respecting bounds).

---

## Observability requirements (decision-linked)
The following telemetry MUST be emitted:
- Gauge: desired replicas (requested vs bounded)
- Counter: bound hit events (`max_hit`, `min_hit`)
- Gauge: forecast freshness and confidence
- Gauge/counter: prediction error (forecast vs realized)
- Counter: decision reason codes (cooldown_blocked, overload_override, predictive_invalid, etc.)
- Gauge: `min_unmet` and associated reason

Metric naming and label limits MUST follow the observability standard referenced in related pages (avoid unbounded cardinality).

---

## Alternatives considered
### A1. Soft bounds (warnings only)
Rejected. Customer requirement is contractual guardrails; soft bounds do not meet budget-capping and baseline guarantees.

### A2. Predictive overrides reactive (prediction wins)
Rejected. Reactive metrics are required to prevent overload when predictions are wrong; predictive must not force scale-down into saturation.

### A3. Clamp first, then compute predictive/reactive
Rejected. Clamping early hides the platform’s “requested desired” intent and reduces auditability (cannot reason about why latency regressed while max-bound was hit).

### A4. Scale-up uses max(predictive, reactive), scale-down uses reactive only
Not selected as the default. We allow predictive input into scale-down only when it is valid and scale-down safety gates pass; however, the net effect is still conservative due to cooldown and overload blocks.

---

## Consequences
### Positive
- Customers get deterministic, enforceable behavior aligned with contracts.
- Support and SRE can quickly diagnose “we hit max” vs “prediction stale” vs “region shortage.”
- Predictive scaling can improve p95 latency during known ramps while maintaining safety.

### Tradeoffs / risks
- Customers can misconfigure bounds (e.g., min too high), increasing shortage risk.
- Hard max may cap performance during unexpected spikes (intentional by contract); requires clear UX and CS guidance.
- Conservative scale-down may increase cost slightly vs aggressive reactive downscaling.

---

## Rollout and compatibility notes
- Existing Dedicated deployments retain current behavior until the feature flag is enabled.
- On enablement, defaults must preserve behavior unless customer explicitly sets bounds.
- During pilot, require SRE readiness review and alert tuning before expanding to additional accounts.

---

## Open questions (tracked outside ADR)
- Exact default cooldowns and step sizes per model family / GPU type (performance tuning doc).
- Whether max should be expressed in replicas, GPUs, or both (schema evolution).
- Smart routing policy interactions during `min_unmet` and `max_hit` states (routing ADR).

---

## Appendix: Reason codes (initial set)
Autoscaler decision records SHOULD include one or more of:
- `PREDICTIVE_VALID`
- `PREDICTIVE_INVALID_STALE`
- `PREDICTIVE_INVALID_LOW_CONFIDENCE`
- `REACTIVE_OVERLOAD_CRITICAL`
- `SCALE_UP`
- `SCALE_DOWN`
- `COOLDOWN_BLOCKED_UP`
- `COOLDOWN_BLOCKED_DOWN`
- `MAX_BOUND_HIT`
- `MIN_BOUND_HIT`
- `MIN_UNMET_REGION_SHORTAGE`
- `MIN_UNMET_PLACEMENT_FAILURE`

(Reason code list is extensible but must remain stable enough for dashboards and runbooks.)

The goal is to provide enterprise-grade, contract-aligned guardrails that are **hard enforced**, **observable**, and **operationally safe**.

---

## Status
**Accepted** (implemented behind feature flags; required for GA).

---

## Context
Redwood Dedicated historically relies on platform-driven autoscaling (reactive metrics + operator overrides). Enterprise customers require:
- A **hard maximum** to prevent unexpected spend and enforce contractual ceilings.
- A **hard minimum** to ensure baseline capacity and avoid cold-start latency.
- Optional **predictive scaling** to pre-warm capacity ahead of known ramps, without sacrificing reliability.

This introduces several ambiguous cases that must be explicitly defined:
- What happens when the platform “wants” to scale outside customer bounds?
- What if predictive suggests scaling down but reactive signals indicate saturation?
- What if the fleet cannot provision the customer minimum due to a region capacity shortage?
- How do we avoid oscillation and unsafe scale-to-zero outcomes?

This ADR clarifies these semantics and the precedence ordering to enable consistent implementation in the autoscaler loop, the control plane policy evaluator, Console UX, and on-call procedures.

---

## Decision
### D1. Customer bounds are **hard constraints** on desired capacity
For a Dedicated deployment with customer bounds:
- Autoscaler MUST NOT set desired replicas below `min_replicas`.
- Autoscaler MUST NOT set desired replicas above `max_replicas`.
- Bounds apply regardless of the source of desired capacity (reactive, predictive, operator, or platform defaults).

**Canonical clamp:**
`bounded_desired = clamp(requested_desired, min_replicas, max_replicas)`

Where:
- `requested_desired` is the desired replica count computed prior to bounds enforcement.
- `bounded_desired` is the desired replica count after applying hard bounds.

### D2. Precedence order for computing requested_desired
The autoscaler computes `requested_desired` using the following precedence and arbitration rules:

`requested_desired` is the desired replica count computed prior to bounds enforcement.
- `bounded_desired` is the desired replica count after applying hard bounds.

### D2. Precedence order for computing requested_desired
The autoscaler computes `requested_desired` using the following precedence and arbitration rules:

1) **Hard safety overrides (scale-up only)**
   - If reactive overload signals exceed critical thresholds (e.g., sustained queue growth / saturation), autoscaler may request an *immediate* scale-up (subject to `max_replicas`).

2) **Predictive desired (if enabled and valid)**
   - If predictive mode is enabled and the forecast is “valid” (fresh, confidence >= minimum, model coverage OK), compute a predictive desired target.

3) **Reactive desired (always available)**
   - Compute reactive desired from observed metrics (queue depth, utilization/saturation, latency signals) using the standard control loop.

4) **Arbitration between predictive and reactive**
   - Requested desired is the **max()** of predictive and reactive desired for scale-up decisions.
   - For scale-down decisions, requested desired is the **min()** of predictive and reactive desired, *subject to scale-down safety rules in D4*.

Rationale: predictive is intended to avoid under-provisioning during ramps, but reactive must still prevent overload if predictions are wrong. For scale-down, we are conservative to prevent churn and under-provisioning.

### D3. Platform defaults do not override explicit customer bounds
Platform defaults (e.g., recommended min, recommended max, default cooldowns) are used only when the customer has not set an explicit value.

Effective policy fields:
- If customer specifies `min_replicas`, it replaces the platform default min.
- If customer specifies `max_replicas`, it replaces the platform default max.
- If a field is unset, platform default applies.

Console MUST display both:
- Customer-configured values (explicit)
- Platform recommended range (informational only)

### D4. Scale-down safety invariants
Scale-down MUST be more conservative than scale-up.

Required invariants:
- Never scale down below `min_replicas`.
- Never scale down if the deployment is in an overload condition (reactive critical signals active).
- Never scale down more than `max_scale_down_step` per control interval.
- Enforce cooldowns and dampening (see D5).

Additionally:
- If predictive returns null/unknown, it MUST NOT contribute to scale-down (treat as “no opinion”).
- If predictive is stale or confidence is below threshold, predictive MUST be ignored (fallback to reactive).

### D5. Anti-oscillation guardrails are mandatory
To prevent oscillation caused by noisy signals or forecast error:
- Enforce separate cooldown windows for scale-up and scale-down (e.g., 60s up, 300s down; exact values may vary by tier but MUST be non-zero).
- Apply smoothing/dampening to reactive signals (e.g., EWMA) and require sustained conditions for scale-down.
- Require minimum step sizing (avoid 1-replica flapping) unless in critical overload.

- Signal inputs and reason codes (predictive_valid, reactive_overload, cooldown_blocked, min_unmet, max_hit)

## Definitions
- **Replicas:** number of serving instances backing a Dedicated deployment (GPU-backed workers).
- **Requested desired:** desired replica count before bounds enforcement.
- **Bounded desired:** desired replica count after hard clamp to [min, max].
- **Reactive signals:** real-time metrics (queue depth, saturation/utilization, latency, error rate) feeding the autoscaler control loop.
- **Predictive signals:** forecasted demand (time-of-day patterns, scheduled events, historical trends) producing a target capacity ahead of observed load.
- **Overload condition:** sustained indicators that the system is under-provisioned (e.g., queue growth + saturation + latency regression).

---

## Precedence and conflict resolution (normative)
### Capacity computation sequence
1. Load effective scaling policy (post-validation).
2. Compute `reactive_desired`.
3. If predictive enabled and forecast valid, compute `predictive_desired`.
4. Compute `requested_desired`:
   - If overload critical: `requested_desired = max(reactive_desired, predictive_desired_if_any)` with overload step-up allowed.
   - Else:
     - For upward moves: `requested_desired = max(reactive_desired, predictive_desired_if_any)`
     - For downward moves: `requested_desired = min(reactive_desired, predictive_desired_if_any)` but blocked by scale-down safety rules.
5. Apply clamp to produce `bounded_desired`.
6. Apply cooldowns / dampening gates.
7. Emit decision record + metrics.

### Bounds enforcement is always last
Bounds are applied after we compute requested desired, but before we actuate scaling.

### Bounds enforcement is always last
Bounds are applied after we compute requested desired, but before we actuate scaling.

This ensures:
- Audit logs can show when the system *wanted* to scale beyond a bound.
- Metrics can track bound-hit rates.

---

## Safety invariants (must-hold)
The following are invariants the autoscaler MUST enforce:
1) **Never exceed max:** `bounded_desired <= max_replicas` at all times.
2) **Never drop below min:** `bounded_desired >= min_replicas` at all times.
3) **No scale-to-zero when bounds enabled:** if `min_replicas >= 1`, scale-to-zero is forbidden.
4) **No unsafe scale-down during overload:** scale-down is blocked when reactive overload signals are active.
5) **Deterministic decisions:** given the same policy + inputs at time T, evaluator yields the same requested/bounded desired and reason codes.
6) **Fallback correctness:** if predictive is unavailable/stale/invalid, behavior equals reactive mode (still respecting bounds).

---

## Observability requirements (decision-linked)
The following telemetry MUST be emitted:
- Gauge: desired replicas (requested vs bounded)
- Counter: bound hit events (`max_hit`, `min_hit`)
- Gauge: forecast freshness and confidence
- Gauge/counter: prediction error (forecast vs realized)
- Counter: decision reason codes (cooldown_blocked, overload_override, predictive_invalid, etc.)
- Gauge: `min_unmet` and associated reason

Metric naming and label limits MUST follow the observability standard referenced in related pages (avoid unbounded cardinality).

---

Rejected. Customer requirement is contractual guardrails; soft bounds do not meet budget-capping and baseline guarantees.
